Universal tricks that work in every semester
Universal tricks that work in every semester
A typical calculation scores 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for correct substitution and 1 mark for the final answer with unit. Always write all three lines, even when you can do it in your head.
Give final answers to 3 significant figures with the correct unit. An answer without a unit can lose the answer mark.
If a later part uses an earlier answer, carry your value forward. Examiners give error-carried-forward (ECF) marks for correct method with a wrong earlier value.
The new format has no choice in Section C: answer every question. Leaving a part blank always scores zero, while a correct formula alone often scores 1 mark.
Check the calculator shows D (degrees). In radian mode, 25.0 sin 15° gives 16.25 instead of 6.47 and every projectile part goes wrong.
Convert every quantity to SI units: mm → m, cm³ → m³, °C → K, g → kg, km → m.
Choose a positive direction (usually upward) and keep to it. A body that lands below its launch point has a negative displacement.
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
Q: positive when heat is supplied to the gas, negative when heat is released.
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
ΔU: positive when temperature rises, negative when temperature falls (ΔU = nC_VΔT, so the sign of ΔT decides it).
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
W (work done BY the gas): positive for expansion, negative for compression, zero at constant volume.
Sign rules for thermodynamics (Q = ΔU + W)
For a complete cycle, ΔU = 0 because the gas returns to its initial state, so net Q = net W.
Body in circular orbit: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r).
Body falling from rest (or launched) over a large height: energy conservation, ½mv² = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Never use v² = u² + 2gh over hundreds of kilometres: g is not constant.

Explain with the aid of a graph: draw and label the graph, AND write the equation for each region with the relationship it gives (e.g. g ∝ r inside, g ∝ 1/r² outside). A graph alone usually scores only half the marks.
Magnitude and direction: always finish with the direction (e.g. "downward"). It carries its own mark.
State two reasons: give two separate, numbered points.
If you start a sentence with "because", finish it. An incomplete reason scores zero.
Each definition below shows the key words the marking scheme looks for. Learn these exactly.
Newton's second law: rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the resultant force and takes place in the direction of the force.
Impulse: product of force and time of action; equals the change in momentum.
Elastic collision: total kinetic energy is conserved (momentum is conserved in every collision).
Work done: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.
Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
Centripetal force: resultant force directed towards the centre of the circular path.
Gravitational field strength: gravitational force per unit mass.
Gravitational potential: work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to that point.
Weightlessness: the body is in free fall (acceleration g) and there is no normal (contact) force on it. Gravity still acts.
Equilibrium: resultant force is zero AND resultant torque about any point is zero.
Centre of gravity: the point where the whole weight appears to act.
Young's modulus: ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the proportional limit.
Elastic limit: the maximum stress beyond which the material does not return to its original length when the load is removed.
Internal energy (ideal gas): the total kinetic energy of the molecules; depends only on temperature.
First law: Q = ΔU + W; heat supplied = increase in internal energy + work done by the gas.
Isothermal: constant temperature, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W. Adiabatic: no heat exchange, so Q = 0 and W = −ΔU.
Conduction: heat transfer from high to low temperature through a medium by vibration of atoms / free electrons, without bulk movement of the medium.
Convection: heat transfer by the bulk movement of a fluid due to density differences. Natural: caused by density differences. Forced: driven by an external device (fan, pump).
Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (infrared); no medium needed.
Thermal conductivity: rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient.

Base quantities are physical quantities that are independent and cannot be defined in terms of other quantities. The seven SI base quantities and units are: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd).
Derived quantities are quantities defined in terms of base quantities by multiplication or division; their units are derived units (e.g. N = kg m s⁻², J = kg m² s⁻², W = kg m² s⁻³, Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²).
Dimension of a physical quantity is the way it is expressed in terms of the base quantities, written in square brackets, e.g. [L], [M], [T].
Homogeneity principle: every term in a physically correct equation must have the same dimensions (and units).
Prefixes: tera T 10¹², giga G 10⁹, mega M 10⁶, kilo k 10³, deci d 10⁻¹, centi c 10⁻², milli m 10⁻³, micro μ 10⁻⁶, nano n 10⁻⁹, pico p 10⁻¹².
Dimensionless quantities (pure numbers, angles in radian, ratios, refractive index, strain) have no unit.
Scalar quantity is a quantity that has magnitude only (e.g. distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature).
Vector quantity is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction (e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum).
Resultant is the single vector that has the same effect as the vectors it replaces.
Vectors are added by the triangle law (head to tail) or the parallelogram law (tail to tail, resultant is the diagonal from the common tail).
Vector subtraction: A − B = A + (−B), where −B has the same magnitude as B but opposite direction.
Resolution of a vector is replacing it by two perpendicular components that together have the same effect.
Unit vector has magnitude 1 and gives direction only; a vector is written A = Aₓi + A_y j.
Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true (accepted) value; it is limited by systematic error.
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another (the spread of readings); it is limited by random error and indicated by a small uncertainty.

Systematic error is an error that makes all readings differ from the true value by the same amount in the same direction (e.g. zero error, wrongly calibrated instrument, parallax by a consistently wrong sight); it cannot be reduced by averaging, but can be corrected by checking zero or calibrating.

Random error is an error that causes readings to scatter above and below the true value in an unpredictable manner (e.g. reaction time, parallax by varying sight); it is reduced by taking many readings and calculating the mean.
Absolute uncertainty Δx is the uncertainty in a measurement, with the same unit; fractional uncertainty is Δx/x; percentage uncertainty is Δx/x × 100%.
Uncertainty of a single reading: analogue instrument ± half of the smallest division (some scales: ± one smallest division); digital instrument ± one smallest digit.
Distance is the total length of the path travelled (scalar); displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position in a stated direction (vector).
Speed is the rate of change of distance; velocity is the rate of change of displacement (vector).
Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one instant, v = ds/dt, the gradient of the displacement–time graph at that instant.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt (vector).
Free fall is motion under gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g = 9.81 m s⁻² near the Earth's surface (air resistance neglected), independent of mass.
A v–t graph: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = displacement (area below the t-axis is negative). An s–t graph: gradient = velocity. An a–t graph: area = change in velocity.
Projectile is an object projected into the air that moves under the action of gravity only (air resistance neglected).
The horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontally constant velocity (aₓ = 0); vertically constant acceleration g downward.
The path (trajectory) of a projectile is a parabola.
At the highest point the vertical component of velocity is zero, the horizontal component is unchanged, and acceleration is g downward.
The speed at the same height on the way up and down is the same; the time of ascent equals the time of descent when landing at the launch level.
A projectile fired horizontally has zero initial vertical velocity; its time of fall depends only on the height h, not on the horizontal speed.

Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant external force. Inertia is the property of a body that resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion; it is measured by mass.
Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force: F = (d(mv))/(dt).
One newton is the resultant force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in the direction of the force.

Newton's third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different bodies, is of the same type and acts along the same line at the same time.
Weight is the gravitational force on a body, W = mg, directed toward the centre of the Earth; mass is the amount of matter and is a scalar that does not change with place.
Apparent weight is the normal reaction exerted on a body, e.g. by a lift floor; it differs from the true weight when the body accelerates vertically.
Linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector with the direction of the velocity, unit kg m s⁻¹ or N s.
Principle of conservation of linear momentum: in an isolated system (no resultant external force), the total linear momentum before an interaction equals the total linear momentum after it.
Impulse is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, and equals the change in linear momentum of the body; it is a vector, unit N s.
Newton's second law (momentum form): the resultant force equals the rate of change of linear momentum.
A force–time graph: the area under the graph equals the impulse (change in momentum); the average force = impulse/time of contact.
Momentum is conserved in all collisions and explosions of an isolated system, whether elastic or inelastic.
Elastic collision is a collision in which both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.
Inelastic collision is a collision in which total linear momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not conserved (some is converted to heat, sound and deformation).

Perfectly (completely) inelastic collision is an inelastic collision in which the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity; the maximum loss of kinetic energy consistent with momentum conservation.
In an elastic collision in one dimension, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.
In a two-dimensional collision, the total momentum is conserved separately along each of two perpendicular axes.
In an explosion, momentum is conserved and kinetic energy increases.
Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between two surfaces in contact; it acts parallel to the surfaces.
Static friction acts when there is no relative motion; it equals the applied force up to a maximum value (limiting friction) Fₘₐₓ = μₛN.
Kinetic (dynamic) friction acts when the surfaces slide; it is approximately constant and independent of speed, F = μₖN, and usually less than the limiting static friction (μₖ < μₛ).
Coefficient of friction is the ratio of the friction force to the normal reaction, μ = F/N; it has no unit and depends on the nature of the surfaces.
Laws of friction: friction is proportional to the normal reaction; it is independent of the area of contact (for the same normal reaction) and, for kinetic friction, independent of speed.
Normal reaction N is the perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface, not always equal to mg.

Work done by a constant force is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement; a scalar, unit joule (J).
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application through 1 m in the direction of the force.
The work done by a variable force is the area under the force–displacement graph, W = ∫F dx.

Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement, zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement (e.g. normal reaction, centripetal force), and negative when the force opposes the displacement (e.g. friction).
Work–energy theorem: the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
A force is conservative if the work done is independent of the path (e.g. gravity, spring force); friction is non-conservative.
Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another, so the total energy of an isolated system is constant.
Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses due to its motion, Eₖ = ½mv².
Gravitational potential energy is the energy a body possesses due to its position in a gravitational field; near the Earth's surface the change in potential energy is ΔU = mgΔh.
Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a deformed spring, U = ½kx².

Conservation of mechanical energy: if only conservative forces do work, the sum of kinetic and potential energy is constant. If friction or air resistance acts, mechanical energy decreases and is converted to heat.
A body released from rest from height h on a smooth surface reaches the bottom with speed v = √2gh, independent of the shape of the path.
Power is the rate of doing work (or the rate of energy transfer), P = W/t; unit watt (W), 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
Instantaneous power is the power at one instant, P = dW/dt = Fv, where v is the velocity in the direction of F.
Average power is the total work done divided by the total time taken.
Efficiency is the ratio of the useful output energy (or power) to the total input energy (or power), usually expressed as a percentage.
The efficiency of a real machine is less than 100% because some energy is lost as heat (friction, resistance) and sound; energy is still conserved.
Kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy: the energy transferred by a power of 1 kW in 1 hour.

Angular displacement θ is the angle swept out by the radius vector from the centre of the circle, measured in radian. 1 rad is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
Angular velocity ω is the rate of change of angular displacement, ω = dθ/dt (rad s⁻¹).
Period T is the time taken for one complete revolution; frequency f is the number of revolutions per unit time, f = 1/T (Hz).
Uniform circular motion is motion in a circle at constant speed. The velocity changes continuously in direction, so the object accelerates.

Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration of an object in circular motion; it is directed towards the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the velocity, and changes the direction of the velocity but not the speed.
Every point on a rigid rotating body has the same ω and T, but the linear speed v increases with distance r from the axis.
Centripetal force is the resultant force directed towards the centre of the circle that is required to make an object move in a circular path; it is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work.
Centripetal force is not a separate force; it is provided by tension, friction, gravitational force, normal reaction or a component of these forces.
Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force; hence a body in circular motion needs a resultant force towards the centre.
Explain the "outward" sensation: it is due to inertia of the body, which tends to continue in a straight line (tangent); there is no real outward force on the body in an inertial frame.
If the centripetal force is removed (string breaks), the object moves along the tangent at constant velocity.

Newton's law of gravitation: every point mass in the universe attracts every other point mass with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
The gravitational force is always attractive, acts along the line joining the two masses, and the two forces form an action–reaction pair (equal magnitude, opposite direction) on the two bodies.
A uniform spherical body acts as if its mass were concentrated at its centre, so r is measured between centres.
Kepler's first law: the orbit of a planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
Kepler's second law: the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
Kepler's third law: the square of the period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of its mean orbital radius (semi-major axis), T² ∝ r³.
Weight is the gravitational force exerted on a body by the Earth; g = GM/R² at the surface.
Gravitational field is a region of space in which a mass experiences a gravitational force.
Gravitational field strength g at a point is the gravitational force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at that point; g is a vector directed towards the mass producing the field.

Gravitational potential V at a point is the work done per unit mass by an external force in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point; V = 0 at infinity, so V is negative everywhere in the field of an attractive mass, and it is a scalar.
Gravitational potential energy U of a mass m at a point is the work done by an external force in bringing the mass from infinity to that point, U = mV.
Field strength is the negative of the potential gradient, g = −dV/dr; the area under a g–r graph gives −ΔV.
Escape speed is the minimum speed at which a body must be projected from the surface of a planet so that it just reaches infinity, where its speed is zero.
An equipotential surface is a surface on which all points have the same potential; no work is done moving a mass along it, and g is perpendicular to it.
Satellite in a circular orbit is moving under the gravitational force of the central body, which provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r.

Geostationary satellite is a satellite that stays above a fixed point on the Earth's equator: it orbits in the equatorial plane, in the same direction as the Earth's rotation (west to east), with period 24 h (same angular velocity as the Earth), at a fixed height of about 3.6×10⁷ m above the surface (r ≈ 4.2×10⁷ m).

Apparent weightlessness: in orbit the satellite and its contents have the same acceleration towards the Earth (free fall), so there is no contact (normal) force between the astronaut and the floor, although the gravitational force still acts.
Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³ for orbits about the same central mass.
The gravitational force on the satellite is perpendicular to its velocity in a circular orbit, so it does no work and the speed and total energy remain constant.
A satellite in a lower orbit has a greater speed and a smaller period; to move to a higher orbit the satellite gains total energy (E becomes less negative).
Torque (moment of a force) about an axis is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force.

Couple is a pair of equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide; it produces rotation without translation, and its torque is the product of one force and the perpendicular distance between the two forces.
Newton's second law of rotation: the angular acceleration of a rigid body about a fixed axis is directly proportional to the resultant torque and inversely proportional to its moment of inertia.
Torque is a vector (clockwise/anticlockwise sense must be stated); a force whose line of action passes through the axis has zero torque.
Angular acceleration α is the rate of change of angular velocity, α = dω/dt (rad s⁻²).

Moment of inertia I of a body about an axis is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis, I = Σmr²; it is the measure of the body's resistance to angular acceleration (rotational inertia).
Moment of inertia depends on the mass, on how the mass is distributed about the axis, and on the position of the axis; the same body has different I about different axes.
Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass: τ = Iα corresponds to F = ma.
A body with its mass distributed further from the axis has a larger I and so is harder to start or stop rotating.
A flywheel has most of its mass at the rim to give a large I, so that it resists changes in angular speed (stores rotational kinetic energy).

Angular momentum L of a rigid body about an axis is the product of its moment of inertia and its angular velocity, L = Iω (kg m² s⁻¹); for a point mass L = mvr.

Principle of conservation of angular momentum: the total angular momentum of a system remains constant if no resultant external torque acts on the system.
7.3 Angular Momentum and Rotational Kinetic Energy
Rotational kinetic energy is the energy a rotating body possesses because of its angular velocity, ½Iω².
7.3 Angular Momentum and Rotational Kinetic Energy
Newton's second law in terms of angular momentum: the resultant torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, τ = dL/dt.

When the moment of inertia of a system decreases (e.g. a skater draws in the arms), ω increases so that L is constant; the rotational kinetic energy increases because work is done by the skater (internal forces).
7.3 Angular Momentum and Rotational Kinetic Energy
In a collision or coupling of rotating bodies about the same axis (inelastic), angular momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is lost.
Translational equilibrium: a body is in translational equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero; it is at rest or moves with constant velocity.
Rotational equilibrium: a body is in rotational equilibrium when the resultant torque about any axis is zero.
Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body (static equilibrium): (1) the vector sum of all forces is zero, and (2) the sum of the moments about any point is zero.
Triangle of forces: if three coplanar forces acting at a point are in equilibrium, they can be represented in magnitude and direction by the three sides of a triangle taken in order.
For three non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action are coplanar and meet at one point (concurrent).
A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces; a body acted on by a couple alone is in translational equilibrium but not in rotational equilibrium.
Moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
Principle of moments: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Centre of gravity of a body is the point through which the whole weight of the body appears to act.
Centre of mass is the point at which the whole mass of the body can be considered to be concentrated; it coincides with the centre of gravity when the gravitational field is uniform.
The centre of gravity of a uniform regular body is at its geometric centre; for a freely suspended body it lies vertically below the point of suspension.

Stable equilibrium: a body returns to its original position after a small displacement; the centre of gravity rises on displacement. Unstable: the body moves further away; the centre of gravity falls. Neutral: the body stays in the new position; the centre of gravity stays at the same height.
A body topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
Stress is the force acting normally per unit cross-sectional area of a material.
Strain is the ratio of the extension to the original length; it has no unit.
Young modulus is the ratio of tensile (or compressive) stress to the corresponding strain, within the limit of proportionality.
Hooke's law: the extension of a material is directly proportional to the applied force provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

Limit of proportionality is the point on the graph beyond which stress is no longer proportional to strain. Elastic limit is the maximum stress beyond which the material does not return to its original length when the force is removed.
Yield point is the point at which the material extends considerably (plastic flow) with little or no increase in stress. Ultimate tensile stress is the maximum stress the material can withstand.

A ductile material shows a large plastic region before fracture (copper, mild steel); a brittle material fractures just after the elastic region with almost no plastic deformation (glass, cast iron); a polymeric material (rubber) shows a large non-linear extension and hysteresis.
Elastic potential energy (strain energy) is the energy stored in a material when it is deformed by a force within the elastic limit.
The work done in stretching a wire equals the area under the force–extension graph; this is stored as elastic potential energy if the elastic limit is not exceeded.
Energy density is the elastic potential energy stored per unit volume of the material.

Beyond the elastic limit, the work done is not wholly stored: part is dissipated as heat during plastic deformation, so the unloading line is not the loading curve (hysteresis for rubber: the area enclosed by the loop is the energy dissipated as heat).
Ideal gas is a gas that obeys the equation of state pV = nRT at all pressures and temperatures.

Boyle's law: for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure is inversely proportional to the volume. Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to the thermodynamic temperature. Pressure law: at constant volume, the pressure is directly proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
Mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kg of carbon-12, i.e. the Avogadro constant N_A of entities.
A real gas behaves like an ideal gas at low pressure and high temperature (molecules far apart, intermolecular forces and molecular volume negligible).
Dalton's law: the total pressure of a mixture of gases equals the sum of the partial pressures of its components.

Assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas: (1) a gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in continuous random motion; (2) the volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container; (3) there are no intermolecular forces except during collisions; (4) collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic; (5) the duration of a collision is negligible …
Pressure of a gas is caused by the molecules colliding with the walls: the rate of change of momentum of the molecules per unit area of the wall.
Root-mean-square speed c_rms is the square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of the molecules.
The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is directly proportional to the thermodynamic temperature, and is independent of the type of gas.
Degrees of freedom f is the number of independent ways in which a molecule can possess energy. Principle of equipartition of energy: each degree of freedom has an average energy of ½kT per molecule.
A monatomic gas has f = 3 (translational), a diatomic gas has f = 5 (3 translational + 2 rotational) at ordinary temperatures, and a polyatomic (non-linear) gas has f = 6.

First law of thermodynamics: the increase in the internal energy of a system is equal to the heat supplied to the system minus the work done by the system on its surroundings (conservation of energy).

Internal energy of a system is the sum of the random kinetic energy and the potential energy of its molecules; for an ideal gas there is no intermolecular potential energy, so U depends only on the thermodynamic temperature.

Heat is the energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference. Work is the energy transferred when the gas expands or is compressed against an external pressure.

Molar heat capacity at constant volume C_V is the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of gas by 1 K at constant volume; at constant pressure Cₚ is the heat required for the same rise at constant pressure; Cₚ is greater than C_V because additional heat is needed for the work done in expansion.
Isothermal process is a process at constant temperature: ΔU = 0, so Q = W; heat absorbed is converted entirely into work done by the gas (pV = constant, Boyle's law).
Adiabatic process is a process in which no heat enters or leaves the system: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W; an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and an adiabatic compression heats it.
Constant-pressure (isobaric) process: W = pΔV, and ΔU = Q − pΔV. Constant-volume (isochoric) process: W = 0, so Q = ΔU, and all the heat supplied increases the internal energy.

Work done by the gas equals the area under the p–V graph; in a cycle, the net work done equals the area enclosed by the loop (clockwise: net work done by the gas; anticlockwise: net work done on the gas).
An adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve through the same point on a p–V graph because γ is greater than 1.
Reversible process is one in which the system passes through a continuous series of equilibrium states and can be returned to the initial state with no change in the surroundings.
Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement of the material, by lattice vibrations of atoms and, in metals, by the collisions of free electrons; it needs a medium.

Convection is the transfer of heat by the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas) caused by density differences; radiation is the transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) and does not need a medium.

Thermal conductivity k is the rate of heat flow through a unit area of a material per unit temperature gradient, i.e. the heat transferred per unit time across unit area when the temperature gradient is 1 K m⁻¹.
Stefan–Boltzmann law: the total power radiated per unit surface area of a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its thermodynamic temperature.
A black body is a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter of radiation at all wavelengths (emissivity e = 1).
Steady state: the temperature at each point does not change with time, so the rate of heat flow is the same through every cross-section in series.

Heat is the energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Radiation transfers it as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) and needs no medium. Power radiated P = eσAT⁴; Wien’s law λmax T = b; a good absorber is a good emitter; net rate P_net = eσA(T₀⁴ − Tₛ⁴).

Equations of motion with constant acceleration
Constant acceleration: a = dv/dt is constant. Integrate from v = u at t = 0: ∫dv = ∫a dt, so v = u + at … (1)
Equations of motion with constant acceleration
v = ds/dt = u + at. Integrate from s = 0 at t = 0: s = ut + ½at² … (2)
Equations of motion with constant acceleration
From (1), t = (v − u)/(a). Substitute into (2): s = (u(v − u))/(a) + (½a(v − u)²)/(a²).
Equations of motion with constant acceleration
Multiply by 2a: 2as = 2uv − 2u² + v² − 2uv + u², so v² = u² + 2as … (3)
Equations of motion with constant acceleration
Area under the v–t graph (a trapezium) gives s = ½(u + v)t … (4)

Learning outcome (a): explain systematic errors and random errors in measurements.
The error in a measurement is decided by the instruments used and the physical constraints of the observer. The two main types are systematic error and random error.
Random error(chance error) is a deviation between an observed value and the true value due to unpredictable and fluctuating factors during measurement.
It makes readings scatter about the true value.
Individual readings may be higher or lower than the true value.
Reduced by taking repeated measurements and using the mean, and by increasing the sample size.
Common sources: parallax errors, the sensitivity of an instrument, the physical constraints of the observer, poorly controlled procedures.

All readings are shifted from the true value by the same amount in the same direction.
Eliminated by improving the measurement method, e.g. using a different instrument.
Common sources: zero errors, instrumental error, incorrect assumptions.

Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true (accepted) value; it is limited by systematic error.
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another (the spread of readings); it is limited by random error and indicated by a small uncertainty.

Systematic error is an error that makes all readings differ from the true value by the same amount in the same direction (e.g. zero error, wrongly calibrated instrument, parallax by a consistently wrong sight); it cannot be reduced by averaging, but can be corrected by checking zero or calibrating.

Random error is an error that causes readings to scatter above and below the true value in an unpredictable manner (e.g. reaction time, parallax by varying sight); it is reduced by taking many readings and calculating the mean.
Absolute uncertainty Δx is the uncertainty in a measurement, with the same unit; fractional uncertainty is Δx/x; percentage uncertainty is Δx/x × 100%.
Uncertainty of a single reading: analogue instrument ± half of the smallest division (some scales: ± one smallest division); digital instrument ± one smallest digit.

Newton’s first lawEvery body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless a net force acts on it. In equation form, ΣF = 0.

The first law tells us what a force does: it changes the state of motion.

Inertia is a body’s reluctance to start moving ("lazy") and its reluctance to stop once it is moving ("hardworking"), so a force is needed to move a body or to stop it.
Inertia depends on mass: mass is a measure of the inertia of a body. A heavy body is harder to move, and harder to stop, than a light one.
When a car stops suddenly the passenger continues to move forward because of his inertia, so a safety belt is needed during emergency braking.

A sphere falling through a fluid
Three forces act: weight W (down), upthrust U (up) and viscous drag F (up). F increases with speed; W and U stay constant.
At the start v = 0, so F = 0. The net force W − U is downwards and the sphere accelerates.
As v increases, F increases, so the net force (W − U − F) and the acceleration decrease. The speed still increases.
When W = U + F, the net force is zero, so by Newton’s second law a = 0. The sphere moves at constant terminal velocity.
The speed never decreases. Write the whole chain: cause → effect → conclusion.

Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant external force. Inertia is the property of a body that resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion; it is measured by mass.
Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force: F = (d(mv))/(dt).
One newton is the resultant force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in the direction of the force.

Newton's third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different bodies, is of the same type and acts along the same line at the same time.
Weight is the gravitational force on a body, W = mg, directed toward the centre of the Earth; mass is the amount of matter and is a scalar that does not change with place.
Apparent weight is the normal reaction exerted on a body, e.g. by a lift floor; it differs from the true weight when the body accelerates vertically.

Elastic collision is a collision in which both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.
Inelastic collision is a collision in which total linear momentum is conserved but total kinetic energy is not conserved (some is converted to heat, sound and deformation).

In a two-dimensional collision, the total momentum is conserved separately along each of two perpendicular axes.

Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between two surfaces in contact; it acts parallel to the surfaces.
Static friction acts when there is no relative motion; it equals the applied force up to a maximum value (limiting friction) Fₘₐₓ = μₛN.
Kinetic (dynamic) friction acts when the surfaces slide; it is approximately constant and independent of speed, F = μₖN, and usually less than the limiting static friction (μₖ < μₛ).
Coefficient of friction is the ratio of the friction force to the normal reaction, μ = F/N; it has no unit and depends on the nature of the surfaces.
Laws of friction: friction is proportional to the normal reaction; it is independent of the area of contact (for the same normal reaction) and, for kinetic friction, independent of speed.
Normal reaction N is the perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface, not always equal to mg.
Static friction grows with the applied force up to μsR; once sliding, kinetic friction μkR is smaller and constant.

Part 1 · Section A: definitions, formulas and traps
Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another, so the total energy of an isolated system is constant.
Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses due to its motion, Eₖ = ½mv².
Gravitational potential energy is the energy a body possesses due to its position in a gravitational field; near the Earth's surface the change in potential energy is ΔU = mgΔh.
Elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a deformed spring, U = ½kx².

Conservation of mechanical energy: if only conservative forces do work, the sum of kinetic and potential energy is constant. If friction or air resistance acts, mechanical energy decreases and is converted to heat.

Energy changes form but the total is conserved; with friction, the energy lost equals the work done against friction.

Escape velocityis the minimum velocity a body needs at the surface of a planet to overcome its gravitational pull and escape completely into space.

Gas molecules in air (average speed about 0.5 km s⁻¹ at s.t.p.; hydrogen about three times faster) are far slower than this, so the Earth keeps its atmosphere.
A planet with a small escape velocity may lose its gases into space and have no atmosphere.

Part 1 · Section A: definitions, formulas and traps
Gravitational field is a region of space in which a mass experiences a gravitational force.
Gravitational field strength g at a point is the gravitational force per unit mass acting on a small test mass placed at that point; g is a vector directed towards the mass producing the field.

Gravitational potential V at a point is the work done per unit mass by an external force in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point; V = 0 at infinity, so V is negative everywhere in the field of an attractive mass, and it is a scalar.
Gravitational potential energy U of a mass m at a point is the work done by an external force in bringing the mass from infinity to that point, U = mV.
Field strength is the negative of the potential gradient, g = −dV/dr; the area under a g–r graph gives −ΔV.
Escape speed is the minimum speed at which a body must be projected from the surface of a planet so that it just reaches infinity, where its speed is zero.
An equipotential surface is a surface on which all points have the same potential; no work is done moving a mass along it, and g is perpendicular to it.
Field strength rises inside the Earth and falls as 1/r² outside; the potential is negative and rises towards zero at infinity.

Part 1 · Section A: definitions, formulas and traps
Angular momentum L of a rigid body about an axis is the product of its moment of inertia and its angular velocity, L = Iω (kg m² s⁻¹); for a point mass L = mvr.
Principle of conservation of angular momentum: the total angular momentum of a system remains constant if no resultant external torque acts on the system.
Rotational kinetic energy is the energy a rotating body possesses because of its angular velocity, ½Iω².
Newton's second law in terms of angular momentum: the resultant torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, τ = dL/dt.

When the moment of inertia of a system decreases (e.g. a skater draws in the arms), ω increases so that L is constant; the rotational kinetic energy increases because work is done by the skater (internal forces).
In a collision or coupling of rotating bodies about the same axis (inelastic), angular momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is lost.
No external torque: angular momentum Iω is conserved, so a smaller moment of inertia gives a faster spin.

Ductile metals: atoms are held by a "sea" of shared electrons that bond equally in every direction. Under tension whole planes of atoms slide past one another (dislocation motion) without breaking the metallic bond, so the metal stretches a long way before fracture.

Brittle materials: strong ionic or covalent bonds hold atoms rigidly and do not allow planes to slide. The bonds stretch only slightly; when those along one plane reach their limit they all snap together and a crack runs straight through.

Polymers: long tangled chain molecules held together by weak van der Waals forces. A small force uncoils and straightens the chains (large extension for little force). Once the chains are aligned, the force acts on the strong covalent bonds along the backbone, so the graph becomes steep: the S-shaped curve.

Stress is the force acting normally per unit cross-sectional area of a material.

In a pot of water heated from below, the heated water at the bottom expands, its density falls and it rises; cooler, denser water sinks to take its place. The water circulates in a convection current.
The fluid moves because of density differences caused by heating. · The fluid is made to move by a pump or a fan.
e.g. warm and cold ocean currents, land and sea breezes, water heated in a pot · e.g. air heated and blown into a room by a fan; car radiator cooling
Radiationis the process by which heat is transferred by electromagnetic waves (infrared, visible light, ultraviolet). It can take place in a vacuum.
All objects radiate energy continuously as electromagnetic waves produced by the thermal motion of their particles.
The wavelengths emitted depend on the temperature: the lower the temperature, the longer the wavelength at which most energy is emitted.
Stefan–Boltzmann lawThe rate of energy radiated per unit surface area of a body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.
e = 0: ideal reflector; e = 1: ideal absorber (a black body). A good absorber is also a good emitter.
An object at T₀ in surroundings at Tₛ also absorbs radiation from them. The net rate of energy radiated is Pₙₑₜ = eσA(T₀⁴ − Tₛ⁴).
Pₙₑₜ positive: net heat flows out and the body cools. Negative: net heat flows in and the body warms.

The Sun sends energy as light and heat. Some is reflected back into space; the rest passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth.
The Earth radiates heat back towards space as infrared radiation (longer wavelength, because the Earth is much cooler than the Sun).

Some gases in the atmosphere (greenhouse gases) absorb this infrared radiation and re-emit part of it back towards the Earth, trapping heat like a blanket. This is the natural greenhouse effect; without it the Earth would be much colder and could not support life.

Global warmingis the increase in the average temperature of the Earth caused by the enhanced greenhouse effect: human activities increase the amount of greenhouse gases, so more heat is trapped and less escapes to space.
The atmosphere traps some of the heat radiated by the Earth. · More greenhouse gases trap more heat.
Some heat still escapes to space. · Less heat escapes to space.
The Earth stays warm enough for life. · The Earth heats up and the climate changes.
The atmosphere is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, which do not trap heat. The greenhouse gases make up less than 1%: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone, water vapour and halocarbons.
Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels (the largest source) and deforestation (fewer trees to absorb CO₂).
Methane: livestock farming, flooded rice fields and decomposing rubbish in landfills; the amount has increased about two and a half times since the Industrial Revolution.
Switch to renewable energy: solar, wind and hydroelectric power instead of fossil fuels.
Improve energy efficiency: energy-saving appliances, insulated buildings, less wasted electricity.
Reduce, reuse and recycle: less waste in landfills, so less methane.
Plant trees (reforestation and afforestation) to absorb carbon dioxide.
Use public transport and electric vehicles to cut emissions.
Support sustainable policies and international agreements to limit greenhouse gas emissions.

On 26 August 2026 part of a glacier on Langtang Lirung, Nepal, collapsed and fell about 1200 m. The ice and rock turned into a debris flow and flash flood that travelled almost 100 km downstream and killed more than 1400 people. Six weeks later, on 11 October, a suspected landslide dam burst on the Budhi Gandaki river and swept away homes and bridges in Gorkha.

The exact cause of the glacier collapse is still being investigated, but scientists are studying the role of warming: the Langtang Lirung glacier retreated by roughly 460 m between 1990 and 2020, and unusually warm conditions were detected around the glacier in the days before it failed.

Part 1 · Section A: definitions, formulas and traps
Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement of the material, by lattice vibrations of atoms and, in metals, by the collisions of free electrons; it needs a medium.

Convection is the transfer of heat by the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas) caused by density differences; radiation is the transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) and does not need a medium.

Thermal conductivity k is the rate of heat flow through a unit area of a material per unit temperature gradient, i.e. the heat transferred per unit time across unit area when the temperature gradient is 1 K m⁻¹.
Stefan–Boltzmann law: the total power radiated per unit surface area of a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its thermodynamic temperature.
A black body is a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter of radiation at all wavelengths (emissivity e = 1).
Steady state: the temperature at each point does not change with time, so the rate of heat flow is the same through every cross-section in series.
Conduction through two layers in series: the rate of heat flow is the same, so the poorer conductor has the steeper temperature gradient.
Black-body radiation curves: a hotter body radiates more at every wavelength and its peak shifts to shorter λ.

Lagged bar: θ against x is a straight line (constant temperature gradient), because no heat is lost from the sides.
Unlagged bar: a curve whose gradient decreases in magnitude along the bar, because heat is lost from the sides so less heat flows further along.

Conduction in non-metals: by lattice vibrations passed from atom to atom. In metals, mainly by free electrons, which move fast and carry energy over long distances; this is why metals are good conductors.

188 definitions, laws and statements, with the key words the marking scheme looks for in bold, chapter by chapter. Taken from the notes, so it always matches them.

Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

The force acts along the line joining the two charges; it is repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges. The two forces form a Newton's third law pair (equal in magnitude, opposite in direction).
Principle of superposition: the net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces exerted on it by each of the other charges separately.
Relative permittivity εᵣ of a medium is the ratio of the force between two charges in a vacuum to the force between the same charges, at the same separation, in the medium (εᵣ = ε/ε₀).
Charge is quantised: Q = ne, where n is an integer.
An electric field is a region in which an electric force acts on a charged body.
Electric field strength at a point is the force per unit positive charge placed at that point (E = F/q); it is a vector quantity whose direction is that of the force on a positive test charge.
Electric field line: a line whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the electric field at that point; the density of the lines is proportional to the field strength.
Field lines begin on positive charges (or at infinity) and end on negative charges (or at infinity); they never cross, because the field has only one direction at a point.
The field of a point charge is radial: outward for a positive charge and inward for a negative charge.
A uniform field exists between two oppositely charged parallel plates: the field lines are parallel and equally spaced, and E has the same value at every point (apart from the edges).
Superposition: the resultant field at a point is the vector sum of the fields due to the individual charges.

Electric flux through a surface is the product of the electric field strength normal to the surface and the area of the surface, Φ = EA cosθ, where θ is the angle between E and the normal to the surface.
Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by ε₀.
The flux depends only on the net enclosed charge, not on the shape or size of the closed surface, and not on the position of the charge inside the surface.
A charge outside the closed surface contributes zero net flux, because every field line that enters the surface also leaves it.
In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside the material of a conductor is zero, so the excess charge lies on the surface of the conductor.
Surface charge density σ is the charge per unit area of a surface, σ = Q/A.
Outside a charged sphere the field is the same as if all the charge were concentrated at the centre.
Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point (V = W/q).
Potential difference between two points is the work done per unit positive charge in moving a test charge from one point to the other.
Electric potential energy of a charge at a point is the work done in bringing the charge from infinity to that point (U = qV).
An equipotential surface is a surface on which all points are at the same potential; no work is done in moving a charge along it, and it is perpendicular to the electric field lines.
The electric field is the negative potential gradient (E = −dV/dr): the field points in the direction of decreasing potential, and its magnitude is large where equipotentials are close together.
Potential is a scalar: the potential due to several charges is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials.
One electron-volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron when it is accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V; 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Capacitance of a capacitor is the ratio of the magnitude of the charge on either plate to the potential difference between the plates (C = Q/V).
One farad is the capacitance of a capacitor that stores a charge of one coulomb when the potential difference across it is one volt (1 F = 1 C V⁻¹).

The capacitance depends only on the geometry of the capacitor (area, separation, shape) and the dielectric between the plates; it does not depend on the charge stored or the potential difference applied.
When a capacitor is connected to a battery the potential difference V is fixed; when it is isolated (disconnected) the charge Q remains constant.
For a parallel plate capacitor the capacitance is directly proportional to the area of the plates and inversely proportional to their separation.

The electric field between the plates is uniform, E = V/d = σ/ε₀, directed from the positive plate to the negative plate; the edge effects are neglected when d is much smaller than the plate dimensions.
If the battery stays connected V is constant, so Q = CV changes when d or A changes; if the capacitor is isolated Q is constant.
A slab of dielectric that partly fills the gap in layers (parallel to the plates) forms capacitors in series; a slab covering part of the area forms capacitors in parallel.
A dielectric is an insulating material which becomes polarised in an electric field.

Relative permittivity (dielectric constant) εᵣ is the ratio of the capacitance of a capacitor with the dielectric between the plates to its capacitance when there is a vacuum between them (εᵣ = C/C₀ = ε/ε₀).

Polarisation: in the external field the molecules of the dielectric become aligned (polar molecules) or stretched (non-polar molecules), so that opposite induced charges appear on the faces of the dielectric.

The induced charges produce an electric field opposite in direction to the applied field, so the net field in the dielectric is reduced (E = E₀/εᵣ), the potential difference between the plates falls for the same charge and so the capacitance increases.
Dielectric breakdown occurs when the field exceeds the dielectric strength of the material and the insulator begins to conduct.

In a parallel combination all capacitors have the same potential difference across them, and the total charge is the sum of the charges on the capacitors.

In a series combination every capacitor carries the same charge, and the total potential difference is the sum of the potential differences across the capacitors.
14.4 Capacitors in Series and in Parallel
The equivalent capacitance in parallel is the sum of the capacitances; in series the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals.
14.4 Capacitors in Series and in Parallel
In series the potential difference across a capacitor is inversely proportional to its capacitance, so the smaller capacitor has the larger potential difference.

The energy stored in a capacitor is the work done in charging it, equal to the area under the graph of potential difference against charge.
14.5 Energy Stored in a Charged Capacitor
Energy density of the electric field is the energy stored per unit volume of the field between the plates.
14.5 Energy Stored in a Charged Capacitor
When a capacitor is charged from a battery through a resistor, the battery supplies energy QV, of which ½QV is stored in the capacitor and ½QV is dissipated as heat in the resistor, independent of R.
14.5 Energy Stored in a Charged Capacitor
When a charged capacitor is connected to an uncharged capacitor the charge is conserved but the total energy decreases; the energy lost is dissipated as heat (and radiation).

The time constant τ = RC is the time taken for the charge on a discharging capacitor to fall to 1/e (about 37%) of its initial value; for charging it is the time for the charge to reach 63% (1 − 1/e) of its final value.
14.6 Charging and Discharging of a Capacitor

During discharge the charge, potential difference and current decay exponentially with time; during charging the current decays exponentially while the charge and potential difference rise exponentially towards their final values.
14.6 Charging and Discharging of a Capacitor

At the start of charging the capacitor has no potential difference, so the initial current is I₀ = V₀/R; when the capacitor is fully charged the current is zero and the potential difference across it equals the EMF.
14.6 Charging and Discharging of a Capacitor
The time constant is increased by increasing R or C; the final charge depends on C and V₀ only.
Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section of a conductor.

Conduction in a metal is due to the free (delocalised) electrons, which have large random thermal velocities in all directions; an applied p.d. sets up an electric field that superimposes a small net drift velocity opposite to the field.
Conventional current is taken in the direction of flow of positive charge, which is opposite to the direction of drift of the electrons.

Explain why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature: the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude, so the free electrons collide with them more frequently; the mean free time between collisions decreases while the free electron density is almost constant.

Explain why the conductivity of a semiconductor increases with temperature: more electrons are released from the covalent bonds, producing more electron-hole pairs; the increase in the number of charge carriers outweighs the increased lattice scattering.
Drift velocity is the mean velocity of the free electrons along the conductor due to the applied electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion.

Why a lamp lights almost instantaneously: the electric field is established along the whole circuit at a speed close to that of light, so the free electrons throughout the wire, including those in the filament, begin to drift at once.
In a steady current the drift velocity is the same at every point of a uniform wire; in a wire of varying cross-section it is greater where the area is smaller.
In a semiconductor both electrons and holes contribute to the current; they drift in opposite directions but their contributions to the conventional current add.
Current density is the current per unit cross-sectional area perpendicular to the direction of the current at that point, J = I/A.
Current density is a vector quantity with the direction of the conventional current.
In a steady current the current I is the same at every cross-section of a conductor, but the current density is greater where the cross-sectional area is smaller.
Ohm's law (microscopic form): the current density in a conductor is directly proportional to the electric field strength, J = σE, at constant temperature.
Analogy: electric current corresponds to the rate of heat flow, and potential difference to temperature difference; conductivity corresponds to thermal conductivity.
Resistivity of a material is the resistance of a wire of that material of unit length and unit cross-sectional area, ρ = RA/L (unit: Ω m).
Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ (unit: Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹ or S m⁻¹); both are properties of the material, not of its size or shape.
Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, G = 1/R (unit: siemens, S = Ω⁻¹).
Ohm’s law: the steady current in a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the physical conditions (such as temperature) remain constant.

A superconductor is a material whose resistivity becomes zero at and below its critical temperature T_c; superconductivity is this phenomenon of zero resistivity below the critical temperature. Uses: strong electromagnets (MRI, particle accelerators), maglev trains and lossless power transmission.
Resistance is the ratio of the potential difference across a conductor to the current through it, R = V/I.

Variation with temperature: for a metal the resistivity increases with temperature because lattice vibrations increase the collision rate; for a semiconductor the resistivity decreases with temperature because the number of charge carriers increases rapidly.
Stretching a wire: at constant volume, if the length is multiplied by k, the area is divided by k, so the resistance is multiplied by k².
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy converted from other forms into electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source; it equals the terminal p.d. when no current flows.
Internal resistance of a source is the resistance to the flow of current within the source itself, arising from the materials of the cell.
Potential difference between two points in a circuit is the electrical energy converted to other forms of energy when a unit charge passes from one point to the other.
A shunt is a resistor of very low resistance connected in parallel with a galvanometer to divert most of the current, converting it into an ammeter.
A multiplier is a resistor of very high resistance connected in series with a galvanometer, converting it into a voltmeter.
Terminal potential difference is the p.d. across the terminals of a source when it delivers current; it is less than the e.m.f. by the 'lost volts' Ir.
Maximum power theorem: the power delivered to the external resistor is maximum when the external resistance equals the internal resistance of the source, R = r.
Cells in series have a total e.m.f. and total internal resistance equal to the sums of the individual values (for cells in the same sense).
Kirchhoff's first law: the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction. It is based on the conservation of charge.
Kirchhoff's second law: in any closed loop the algebraic sum of the e.m.f.s equals the algebraic sum of the products IR (potential drops) in the loop. It is based on the conservation of energy.

Sign convention: choose a direction for each current and for the loop; an e.m.f. is positive if the loop direction passes through the cell from the negative to the positive terminal, and IR is positive if the loop direction is the same as the current direction.
Opposing cells in a loop give a net e.m.f. equal to the difference of the e.m.f.s.

A potential divider is a circuit in which two or more resistors in series are connected across a supply so that the supply voltage is shared in proportion to the resistances; the output is taken across one of them.
Output voltage is directly proportional to the resistance across which it is taken, so the larger resistor receives the larger share.
Loading effect: a load connected in parallel with the output resistor reduces the effective resistance of that arm, so the output p.d. decreases below the no-load value.

Sensors: the resistance of a thermistor (NTC) decreases as temperature increases, and the resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases; the p.d. across the sensor in a divider therefore decreases.
A rheostat as a potential divider has its whole track across the supply, which allows the output to vary continuously from zero to the supply p.d.

A potentiometer is a device used to measure the e.m.f. of a cell, or to compare e.m.f.s, by balancing the p.d. across a length of uniform wire against the e.m.f. of the cell, so that no current is drawn from the cell at balance.
At the balance point the galvanometer reads zero, so there is no current in the galvanometer branch and no p.d. across it.
The potentiometer is more accurate than a voltmeter because at balance no current is drawn from the cell, so the measured value equals the e.m.f. and not the terminal p.d.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the galvanometer reads zero, which occurs when the ratio of the resistances in one arm equals the ratio in the other, P/Q = R/S.
At balance the two points connected to the galvanometer are at the same potential.
Magnetic field is a region in which a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnetic material experiences a magnetic force.

Magnetic field lines are lines whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field (flux density) at that point; outside a magnet they are directed from the north pole to the south pole.
Magnetic flux density, B, is the force acting per unit length on a straight conductor carrying a current of 1 A that is placed perpendicular to the magnetic field.
One tesla is the magnetic flux density that produces a force of 1 N on 1 m of straight conductor carrying a current of 1 A perpendicular to the field.
For a moving charge: B is the force per unit charge per unit velocity on a charge moving perpendicular to the field, B = (F)/(qv sin θ).
Relative permeability μ_r of a medium is the ratio of the permeability of the medium to the permeability of free space, μ_r = μ/μ₀.
Magnetic field lines always form closed loops (no magnetic monopoles); they never cross; the closer the lines, the stronger the field.
A magnetic field is produced by a moving charge (a current) or by a permanent magnet; a stationary charge produces only an electric field.

Right-hand grip rule (straight wire): grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing along the conventional current; the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines (concentric circles around the wire).
Magnetic force on a moving charge: a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences a force of magnitude F = qvB sinθ, which is perpendicular to both v and B.
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and does not change the speed or kinetic energy of the particle; it changes only the direction of motion.

When v is perpendicular to B, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force and the particle moves in a circle; when v is parallel (or antiparallel) to B, the force is zero and the motion is a straight line; at other angles the path is a helix.

Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = direction of B, second finger = direction of conventional current (direction of motion of a positive charge), thumb = direction of force. For a negative charge the second finger points opposite to its velocity.
Positive and negative charges of the same velocity are deflected in opposite directions.
Velocity selector: in perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, a particle passes undeflected when qE = qvB, so only particles of speed v = E/B emerge.
A straight conductor of length L carrying a current I in a magnetic field B experiences a force F = BIL sinθ, perpendicular to both the conductor and the field.
Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field B, second finger = conventional current I, thumb = force F (motion); the three are mutually perpendicular.
The force is a maximum (BIL) when the conductor is perpendicular to B and zero when the conductor is parallel to B.
The force arises because the field exerts a force on each moving charge carrier; the sum over all the carriers in the length L gives the force on the conductor.

A rectangular coil of N turns in a uniform field experiences no net force but a torque τ = NIAB sinφ, where φ is the angle between the normal to the coil and B (equivalently NIAB cosα where α is the angle between the plane of the coil and B).
The torque is a maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B and zero when the plane is perpendicular to B; this is the principle of the moving-coil meter and the d.c. motor.
Ampère’s law: for any closed path, the sum of the products of the length elements Δl and the component of B parallel to them equals μ₀ times the current enclosed by the path, ΣB_∥Δl = μ₀I.
Right-hand grip rule (straight wire): thumb along the conventional current, fingers curl in the direction of B.
Right-hand grip rule (coil/solenoid): fingers curl in the direction of the current, thumb points along B inside the coil, i.e. towards the north-pole end.
The field of a long straight wire consists of concentric circles; B is inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance r.
The field inside a long solenoid (far from the ends) is uniform and parallel to the axis; the field outside is very small.
Superposition: the resultant field at a point is the vector sum of the fields produced by each current; fields from different wires may cancel at a neutral point.
Two coaxial coils or concentric coils with opposing currents give zero net field at the centre when their individual fields are equal in magnitude.
The field of one wire exerts a force on the current in the other; by Newton's third law the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever the sizes of the currents.
Parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other; wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel each other.

The ampere is that constant current which, if maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible cross-section placed one metre apart in a vacuum, produces a force of 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre of length between them.
Explanation: wire 1 produces a field B₁ = (μ₀I₁)/(2πd) at wire 2; the force on wire 2 is F = B₁I₂L, directed by Fleming's left-hand rule towards wire 1 when the currents are parallel.
The tesla is the magnetic flux density that gives a force of 1 N per metre on a conductor carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field.
Specific charge of the electron is the ratio of its charge to its mass, e/m (C kg⁻¹).
Thomson's method: electrons are accelerated and pass through crossed electric and magnetic fields; the fields are adjusted so that the beam is undeflected, so that eE = evB, giving v = E/B.
With the electric field switched off, the magnetic force makes the electrons move in a circular arc: evB = mv²/r, so e/m = v/(Br).
Alternative method: electrons accelerated through p.d. V gain kinetic energy eV = ½mv²; combined with r = mv/eB this gives e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
The experiment determines the ratio e/m only; the charge e must be found independently (Millikan's oil-drop experiment) to find m.
The ratio e/m for cathode rays is the same for all cathode materials, showing that electrons are a universal constituent of matter.

Hall effect is the production of a potential difference (Hall voltage) across a current-carrying conductor or semiconductor placed in a magnetic field, the potential difference being perpendicular to both the current and the field.

Hall voltage is the transverse potential difference produced across a current-carrying conductor when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the current, as the drifting charge carriers are deflected by the magnetic force.
Explanation: the magnetic force deflects the moving charge carriers to one side of the slab; the accumulated charge sets up a transverse electric field E_H.
The Hall voltage reaches a steady value when the electric force on a carrier balances the magnetic force: eE_H = evB.

The sign of the Hall voltage identifies the sign of the charge carriers: with the same current direction and field direction, electrons and holes are deflected to the same side but give opposite polarity across the slab (use Fleming's left-hand rule with conventional current).
In a semiconductor the carrier density n is much lower than in a metal, so V_H is much larger.
Application: a Hall probe measures B because V_H ∝ B at constant current; it is made from a thin semiconductor slab for a large V_H.

Magnetic flux through a surface is the product of the magnetic flux density and the area of the surface, measured perpendicular to the field, Φ = BA cosθ; it can be pictured as the total number of magnetic field lines passing through the area.
Weber (Wb) is the magnetic flux when a magnetic flux density of 1 T passes perpendicularly through an area of 1 m².
Magnetic flux linkage is the product of the number of turns of a coil and the magnetic flux through each turn, NΦ.
Magnetic flux density B is the magnetic flux per unit area perpendicular to the field (the number of field lines per unit normal area), unit tesla (T = Wb m⁻²).
For a non-uniform field, the flux is found by summing the normal component of B over all area elements, Φ = ∫B·dA.
Faraday's law: the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage (or the rate of cutting of magnetic flux).
Electromagnetic induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. (and an induced current in a closed circuit) when the magnetic flux linked with a conductor changes.
Induced e.m.f. is the e.m.f. produced in a conductor when there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with it.
Lenz's law: the direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy: work must be done against the opposing effect to produce the induced current.
Induced e.m.f. appears whenever the flux linkage changes, by changing B, A or θ, whether or not the circuit is closed; an induced current flows only in a closed circuit.
For a straight conductor moving across a uniform field, the induced e.m.f. is the product of B, the length of the conductor and the velocity perpendicular to B.
Self-induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. in a coil due to a change in the current in the same coil, which changes the magnetic flux linked with it.
Self-inductance L of a coil is the ratio of the magnetic flux linkage in the coil to the current flowing through it, L = NΦ/I.
Henry (H) is the self-inductance of a coil in which an e.m.f. of 1 V is induced when the current changes at the rate of 1 A s⁻¹.
Self-inductance can also be defined as the back e.m.f. induced in a coil per unit rate of change of current in the coil, L = −ε/dI/dt.
Back e.m.f. is the induced e.m.f. produced in a circuit by a change in its own current; it opposes the change in current that produces it (Lenz’s law).
By Lenz's law, the self-induced e.m.f. always opposes the change in current: it opposes an increase in current and opposes a decrease in current.
The self-induced e.m.f. is large when the current is switched off very quickly, since dI/dt is large; this explains the spark across the switch contacts.
The energy stored in an inductor is the work done against the self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current; it is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor.
The energy is released when the current decreases, as the self-induced e.m.f. then maintains the current for a short time.
The energy stored per unit volume of a magnetic field is the energy density, u = B²/2μ₀.
Energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor, not lost; in an ideal inductor there is no energy dissipation.
Mutual induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. in one coil due to a change in the current in a neighbouring coil, which changes the magnetic flux linked with the first coil.
Mutual inductance M is the ratio of the magnetic flux linkage in one coil to the current in the other coil that produces the flux, M = (N₂Φ₂₁)/(I₁).
Henry (H) is the mutual inductance of two coils when a current changing at the rate of 1 A s⁻¹ in one coil induces an e.m.f. of 1 V in the other.
Mutual inductance can also be defined as the e.m.f. induced in one coil per unit rate of change of current in the other coil, M = −ε₂/dI₁/dt.
Mutual inductance depends on the geometry of the coils (number of turns, size, separation, relative orientation) and the permeability of the core, not on the current.
Transformer: an alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in the core, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil by mutual induction.
An alternating current is a current that reverses its direction at a constant frequency; usually it varies sinusoidally with time, I = I₀ sinωt.
Root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current is the value of the steady direct current that dissipates heat in a given resistor at the same rate as the alternating current.
In a pure resistor, the current is in phase with the voltage.
The instantaneous power P = I²R varies with a frequency twice that of the current and is always non-negative; the mean power is half the peak power.
Peak value: the maximum magnitude of the current or voltage during a cycle.
Inductive reactance X_L is the opposition of an inductor to alternating current, given by the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the inductor to the r.m.s. (or peak) current through it.
In a pure inductor, the current lags the applied voltage by 90° (π/2 rad).
The mean power dissipated in a pure inductor is zero over one complete cycle, because energy is stored in the magnetic field and returned to the source alternately.
At very high frequency, the inductor opposes the current strongly; for direct current (f = 0), X_L = 0 and the inductor offers no opposition (apart from its resistance).
Capacitive reactance X_C is the opposition of a capacitor to alternating current, given by the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the capacitor to the r.m.s. (or peak) current through it.
In a pure capacitor, the current leads the applied voltage by 90° (π/2 rad).
The mean power dissipated in a pure capacitor is zero over one complete cycle, because energy is stored in the electric field and returned to the source alternately.
A capacitor blocks direct current (X_C → as f → 0) and passes high-frequency alternating current more easily (X_C → 0 as f → ).
Impedance Z is the total opposition of an a.c. circuit to the alternating current; it is the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the circuit to the r.m.s. (or peak) current in it.
In a series R-L circuit, the voltage leads the current by a phase angle φ; in a series R-C circuit, the current leads the voltage by φ, where 0° < φ < 90°.
Power factor is the ratio of the mean power dissipated to the product of V_rms and I_rms, equal to cosφ = R/Z.
The mean power is dissipated only in the resistance; the inductor and capacitor dissipate no mean power.
The voltages across R and L (or C) are 90° out of phase, so the supply voltage is their phasor (vector) sum and not their arithmetic sum.

Heating the air raises the mean kinetic energy of its molecules; at the same pressure the hot air is less dense (pV = nRT), so the balloon is pushed up by the cooler, denser air around it.

Release the bottle and the air expands again, so the diver rises. A submarine’s ballast tanks use the same idea.

Work done by a gas is the area under the p–V graph (W = ∫p dV), and Q = ΔU + W. Constant volume: W = 0. Constant pressure: W = pΔV = nRΔT. Isothermal: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), ΔU = 0. Adiabatic: W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ − 1), Q = 0. With worked examples.
