Air is compressed so quickly that little heat escapes (nearly adiabatic): work done on the gas raises its internal energy and temperature enough to ignite the fuel without a spark.

Heat is the energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Radiation transfers it as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) and needs no medium. Power radiated P = eσAT⁴; Wien’s law λmax T = b; a good absorber is a good emitter; net rate P_net = eσA(T₀⁴ − Tₛ⁴).

The Sun (≈ 5800 K) emits short-wavelength radiation that warms the Earth’s surface. The cooler surface (≈ 288 K) emits long-wavelength infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit, partly back to the surface. More greenhouse gases from human activities give the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.

Does the Burj Khalifa collect lightning for electricity?
Being the tallest structure for miles, the Burj Khalifa is struck by lightning during thunderstorms. In Richard Hammond’s BIG, Richard climbs to its lightning conductor at the very top.
Does the Burj Khalifa collect lightning for electricity?

A common misconception: the tower does not collect lightning to use as electricity. The lightning protection system safely carries the charge to earth. The tower’s steel frame also acts as a Faraday cage, so the current flows around the outside and the people inside are safe. No one has yet found a practical way to store the energy of lightning.

Electric flux through a surface is the product of the electric field strength normal to the surface and the area of the surface, Φ = EA cosθ, where θ is the angle between E and the normal to the surface.
Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by ε₀.
The flux depends only on the net enclosed charge, not on the shape or size of the closed surface, and not on the position of the charge inside the surface.
A charge outside the closed surface contributes zero net flux, because every field line that enters the surface also leaves it.
In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside the material of a conductor is zero, so the excess charge lies on the surface of the conductor.
Surface charge density σ is the charge per unit area of a surface, σ = Q/A.
Outside a charged sphere the field is the same as if all the charge were concentrated at the centre.

When S is closed, electrons flow from the negative terminal of the battery, through R, onto plate B. Electrons leave plate A for the positive terminal, so A becomes positive.
At the start the capacitor is uncharged, so the whole e.m.f. is across R: the current is largest, I₀ = V₀/R.
As charge builds up, the p.d. across C rises, so the p.d. across R (and the current) falls.

When S is closed, electrons flow from plate B through R to plate A and neutralise its positive charge.
At the start the p.d. is V₀, so the current is largest, I₀ = V₀/R.
As the charge falls, the p.d. falls, so the current falls. Discharging ends when Q = 0, V = 0 and I = 0.
The current flows in the opposite direction to the charging current.

Time constant, τof an RC circuit: the time for the charge (or current) to fall to 1/e (37%) of its initial value during discharging. During charging, it is the time for the charge to rise to (1 − 1/e), 63% of its final value.
At t = τ: e⁻¹ = 0.37, so discharging gives Q = 0.37Q₀; charging gives Q = 0.63Q₀ and I = 0.37I₀.
After about 5τ the capacitor is practically fully charged (99.3%) or fully discharged.

A dielectric is an insulating material which becomes polarised in an electric field.

Relative permittivity (dielectric constant) εᵣ is the ratio of the capacitance of a capacitor with the dielectric between the plates to its capacitance when there is a vacuum between them (εᵣ = C/C₀ = ε/ε₀).

Polarisation: in the external field the molecules of the dielectric become aligned (polar molecules) or stretched (non-polar molecules), so that opposite induced charges appear on the faces of the dielectric.

The induced charges produce an electric field opposite in direction to the applied field, so the net field in the dielectric is reduced (E = E₀/εᵣ), the potential difference between the plates falls for the same charge and so the capacitance increases.
Dielectric breakdown occurs when the field exceeds the dielectric strength of the material and the insulator begins to conduct.

14.4 Capacitors in Series and in Parallel
In a parallel combination all capacitors have the same potential difference across them, and the total charge is the sum of the charges on the capacitors.
In a series combination every capacitor carries the same charge, and the total potential difference is the sum of the potential differences across the capacitors.
The equivalent capacitance in parallel is the sum of the capacitances; in series the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals.
In series the potential difference across a capacitor is inversely proportional to its capacitance, so the smaller capacitor has the larger potential difference.
Series capacitors share the same charge; parallel capacitors share the same p.d.

Simple d.c. circuits can be simplified: read the words given, redraw the circuit by following the current from the positive terminal, then combine series and parallel parts. Use Kirchhoff’s laws only for complex circuits that cannot be simplified.
Maximum power is delivered to the external resistor when R = r. In an MCQ, check first for a short circuit before calculating every option.

An ammeter has a very low resistance (shunt in parallel); a voltmeter has a very high resistance (multiplier in series). Shunt: V_shunt = V_meter; multiplier: same current, V = V_meter + V_multiplier.
Kirchhoff's first law: the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction. It is based on the conservation of charge.
Kirchhoff's second law: in any closed loop the algebraic sum of the e.m.f.s equals the algebraic sum of the products IR (potential drops) in the loop. It is based on the conservation of energy.

Sign convention: choose a direction for each current and for the loop; an e.m.f. is positive if the loop direction passes through the cell from the negative to the positive terminal, and IR is positive if the loop direction is the same as the current direction.
Opposing cells in a loop give a net e.m.f. equal to the difference of the e.m.f.s.
Kirchhoff's laws: current in = current out at a junction; round a loop Σε = ΣIR.
Kirchhoff's first law (junction rule) · ΣI_in = ΣI_out · I = current (A); applies at a junction
Kirchhoff's second law (loop rule) · ΣE = ΣIR · E = e.m.f. (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); applies around a closed loop
Resistors in series · R = R₁ + R₂ + … · R = total resistance (Ω)
Resistors in parallel · 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … · R = total resistance (Ω)
Resistor with a voltmeter across it · (RR_V)/(R + R_V) · R_V = finite resistance of the voltmeter (Ω); R = resistor (Ω); combined resistance when the voltmeter is connected across R
Draw the circuit with labelled currents and a chosen loop direction before writing the equations.
Write the junction equation and one loop equation per independent loop, then solve the simultaneous equations.
State the direction of each current found; a negative answer means the current flows opposite to the direction assumed.
For a real voltmeter, replace the resistor and voltmeter by their parallel equivalent before applying the potential divider rule.
You may choose any direction for each current and any loops; a correct method gives the same final answer. Write the first law (junction) and second law (loop) equations clearly, as each earns marks.
To find the potential at a point, start from a point of known potential (e.g. earthed = 0 V) and add or subtract the e.m.f.s and IR drops along the path.

A potential divider is a circuit in which two or more resistors in series are connected across a supply so that the supply voltage is shared in proportion to the resistances; the output is taken across one of them.
Output voltage is directly proportional to the resistance across which it is taken, so the larger resistor receives the larger share.
Loading effect: a load connected in parallel with the output resistor reduces the effective resistance of that arm, so the output p.d. decreases below the no-load value.

Sensors: the resistance of a thermistor (NTC) decreases as temperature increases, and the resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases; the p.d. across the sensor in a divider therefore decreases.
A rheostat as a potential divider has its whole track across the supply, which allows the output to vary continuously from zero to the supply p.d.
Potential divider: Vout = Vin R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Potential divider output · V_out = V_in × (R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) · V_out = output p.d. (V); V_in = input p.d. (V); R₂ = resistor across which the output is taken (Ω); R₁ = other resistor (Ω)
Ratio of output to input · (V_out)/(V_in) = (R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) · Ratio is dimensionless
Voltage ratio in series · V₁ : V₂ = R₁ : R₂ · For resistors in series
Divider with a load · R₂ → (R₂R_L)/(R₂ + R_L) · R_L = load resistance (Ω); replace R₂ by this combination in the formula
Current in the divider · I = (V_in)/(R₁ + R₂); V = IR · I = current (A); V = p.d. across each resistor (V), using its own R
Identify the resistor across which the output is taken, then write Vout = Vin × (R)/(R₁ + R₂) and substitute.
For sensor questions, state the change of resistance, then the change of its fraction of the total resistance, then the change of the output p.d.
For loading, combine the load and output resistor in parallel first, then recalculate the ratio.
Give the voltage in V to 3 s.f.; resistances in kΩ may be used directly if they are consistent, as the ratio is dimensionless.

A potentiometer is a device used to measure the e.m.f. of a cell, or to compare e.m.f.s, by balancing the p.d. across a length of uniform wire against the e.m.f. of the cell, so that no current is drawn from the cell at balance.
At the balance point the galvanometer reads zero, so there is no current in the galvanometer branch and no p.d. across it.
The potentiometer is more accurate than a voltmeter because at balance no current is drawn from the cell, so the measured value equals the e.m.f. and not the terminal p.d.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the galvanometer reads zero, which occurs when the ratio of the resistances in one arm equals the ratio in the other, P/Q = R/S.
At balance the two points connected to the galvanometer are at the same potential.
Potentiometer: at balance no current flows through the galvanometer; Wheatstone bridge balances when P/Q = R/S.
Potentiometer balance length · E ∝ l; E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ · l = balance length (cm or m); for a uniform wire with a constant driver current
E.m.f. from balance length · E = l/LV₀ · L = total wire length (same unit as l); V₀ = p.d. across the whole wire (V)
P.d. across the wire · V₀ = IR_wire · I = driver current (A); R_wire = resistance of the wire (Ω)
Driver circuit current · I = (E_driver)/(R + R_wire + r) · E_driver = e.m.f. of the driver cell (V); R = series resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω)
Wheatstone bridge balance · P/Q = R/S · P, Q, R, S = resistances of the four arms (Ω); at balance
Slide-wire bridge · R/X = l₁/l₂ · X = unknown resistance (Ω); l₁, l₂ = lengths of the wire on either side of the balance point; resistance is proportional to length for a uniform wire
State that E is proportional to the balance length because the wire is uniform and carries a constant current.
Write E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂, substitute the lengths and then calculate the unknown e.m.f. with unit.
Explain zero deflection by stating that there is no current through the galvanometer, hence no current drawn from the cell.
For the Wheatstone bridge, write the balance condition first, identify the correct arms, then solve for the unknown resistance.

Driver cell only across the wire: use V ∝ l directly. Driver cell with a resistance in series (or internal resistance): first find the current in the driver circuit, I = E/(Rₜₒₜₐₗ), then the p.d. per unit length, then the balance length.

Meter bridge: keep the balance length between 30 cm and 70 cm, and interchange the two resistors and repeat to cancel end errors. A Wheatstone bridge works only when the ratio of resistances on either side of the galvanometer is equal.

Magnetic fielda region of space where a magnetic force is experienced by a magnetic material, a current-carrying conductor or a moving charge. It is a field of force produced by permanent magnets or by current-carrying conductors.
A magnet has two poles, north (N) and south (S). Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
The direction of the field at a point is the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle points when placed there.
Field patterns are shown with iron filings or a plotting compass.
Field lines go from N to S outside a magnet (and S to N inside it), so they form closed loops.
The tangent to a line at a point gives the direction of the field there.
Field lines never cross (the field has only one direction at each point).
The closer the lines, the stronger the field: the number of lines per unit area is proportional to the field strength.
Figure 17.1: a uniform field and a non-uniform field.
Figure 17.2: a field perpendicular to the page.
Figure 17.4: two like poles facing each other. At the neutral point the two fields cancel.
Figure 17.5: a long straight wire: concentric circles. Right-hand grip rule.
Figure 17.6: a solenoid: like a bar magnet outside, uniform inside.

Long straight wire: concentric circles centred on the wire, further apart away from the wire (weaker field). Direction: right-hand grip rule, thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of B.
Flat circular coil: near the centre the lines are almost straight and perpendicular to the coil; the coil behaves like a short magnet.
Solenoid: outside, like a bar magnet; inside, the field is uniform and parallel to the axis. The end where the current flows anticlockwise (seen from outside) is a north pole.
The Earth has a field like a large bar magnet whose south pole is near the geographic north pole, so a compass needle points north.
A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B feels a force that is perpendicular to both v and B.
Magnetic flux density, Bdefined by F = qvB sin θ: B = (F)/(qv sin θ). One tesla is the flux density in which a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to the field feels a force of 1 N.
Unit: tesla (T) = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = Wb m⁻². B is a vector, along the field lines.
F = 0 when the charge is at rest (v = 0) or moves parallel to B (θ = 0° or 180°).
F is greatest, qvB, when the charge moves perpendicular to B.
Figure 17.7: Fleming's left-hand rule. For a positive charge the second finger points along v; for a negative charge (electron) it points opposite to v.
If v is parallel (or antiparallel) to B, sin θ = 0, so there is no magnetic force. The charge carries on in a straight line at constant speed.
Figure 17.8: circular motion of a charge in a uniform magnetic field.
A faster particle moves in a larger circle, but the period does not depend on the speed.
A positive and a negative charge with the same speed curve in opposite directions.

Choose the sign of the charge, its speed and the flux density. Perpendicular to B it moves in a circle: watch the radius change with v and B while the time for one turn depends only on B. Then switch to "parallel to B".
A current is a stream of moving charges. Each charge feels a force qvB sin θ, and the forces on all the charges in the wire add up to a force on the wire.
Figure 17.9: a length l of wire in a uniform field.
Direction: Fleming's left-hand rule with the second finger along the current.
This is the principle of the electric motor and the moving-coil meter.
Ampère's lawthe line integral of B around any closed loop is equal to μ₀ times the current enclosed by the loop.
Applying Ampère's law to a long straight wire
Applying Ampère's law to a long straight wire
Applying Ampère's law to a long straight wire
Figure 17.10: a circular Amperian loop around a long straight wire.
Long straight wire · B = μ₀I/2πr · r = perpendicular distance from the wire
Flat circular coil, at its centre · B = (μ₀NI)/(2r) · N turns of radius r
Long solenoid, inside · B = μ₀nI · n = N/L = turns per unit length
Figure 17.11: two long parallel wires a distance d apart.

With I₁ = I₂ = 1 A and d = 1 m: F/l = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹. This was used to define the ampere: the constant current which, in each of two infinitely long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section 1 m apart in a vacuum, gives a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length.

Change the size and direction of each current and the separation. See the field of each wire at the other one and the forces: same direction attract, opposite directions repel. The forces are always equal and opposite.

When E, B and v are perpendicular to each other, the electric and magnetic forces on a charge are in opposite directions. If they are equal, the resultant force is zero and the charge goes straight through, undeflected.
Figure 17.12: a velocity selector. Only particles with v = E/B pass straight through; the result does not depend on q or m.
Faster particles: qvB > qE, they bend towards the magnetic force. Slower particles bend towards the electric force.
This arrangement is a velocity selector (used, for example, before the magnetic field of a mass spectrometer).
Fire electrons through the plates. Adjust E and B until the beam goes straight through (v = E/B). Then switch off E: the beam bends into a circle, and its radius gives e/m.
A real use: the mass spectrometer
A real use: the mass spectrometer
A real use: the mass spectrometer

Choose an element and watch its isotopes leave the velocity selector at the same speed and then separate in the magnetic field B₂. Change B₂: a stronger field makes smaller circles and brings the isotopes closer together on the detector.

Hall effectwhen a current flows through a conductor or semiconductor in a magnetic field perpendicular to the current, a p.d. (the Hall voltage) appears across the sides of the specimen, perpendicular to both the current and the field.
Figure 17.14: the Hall effect in a slab with electrons as charge carriers.
How the Hall voltage builds up
How the Hall voltage builds up
V_H ∝ 1/n. Metals have a very large n, so their Hall voltage is tiny. Semiconductors have a much smaller n, so V_H is large enough to measure: Hall probes use semiconductors.
A thin specimen (small t) gives a larger V_H.
Measuring magnetic flux density with a Hall probe: with I constant, V_H ∝ B. The probe is small, so it can measure B at a point, and it responds quickly to changing fields.
Finding the sign of the charge carriers: the side that becomes positive shows whether the carriers are electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type).
Finding the number density n of the carriers: n = BI/(eV_Ht).
Hall sensors in everyday devices: measuring current without breaking the circuit, detecting the speed of a rotating wheel, and as contactless switches.

Choose electrons or holes as the charge carriers and change B and the current. Watch the carriers pile up on one face until the Hall voltage stops further build-up. The sign of the top face tells you the sign of the carriers.

A current in a superconducting solenoid produces a very strong uniform magnetic field (B = μ₀nI); steel objects are pulled in with great force.
Magnetic field is a region in which a moving charge, a current-carrying conductor or a magnetic material experiences a magnetic force.

Magnetic field lines are lines whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field (flux density) at that point; outside a magnet they are directed from the north pole to the south pole.
Magnetic flux density, B, is the force acting per unit length on a straight conductor carrying a current of 1 A that is placed perpendicular to the magnetic field.
One tesla is the magnetic flux density that produces a force of 1 N on 1 m of straight conductor carrying a current of 1 A perpendicular to the field.
For a moving charge: B is the force per unit charge per unit velocity on a charge moving perpendicular to the field, B = (F)/(qv sin θ).
Relative permeability μ_r of a medium is the ratio of the permeability of the medium to the permeability of free space, μ_r = μ/μ₀.
Magnetic field lines always form closed loops (no magnetic monopoles); they never cross; the closer the lines, the stronger the field.
A magnetic field is produced by a moving charge (a current) or by a permanent magnet; a stationary charge produces only an electric field.

Right-hand grip rule (straight wire): grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing along the conventional current; the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines (concentric circles around the wire).
Magnetic field lines run from the N pole to the S pole outside a magnet and never cross.
Magnetic flux density · B = (F)/(IL sinθ) · B = magnetic flux density (T); F = force (N); I = current (A); L = length of conductor in the field (m); θ = angle between the conductor and B
Tesla · 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 Wb m⁻² · T = tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density; Wb = weber
Magnetic field of a straight wire · B = μ₀I/2πr · I = current (A); r = perpendicular distance from the wire (m); μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹ (T m A⁻¹)
Define B by quoting the force on a conductor: "force per unit current per unit length, conductor perpendicular to the field".
When asked to sketch a field pattern: draw closed lines with arrows, closer together where the field is stronger, and label N and S poles or the current direction.
For a wire, state "concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire, getting further apart as r increases".
State the direction rule used (right-hand grip) and the direction of the current in the same answer.
Magnetic force on a moving charge: a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences a force of magnitude F = qvB sinθ, which is perpendicular to both v and B.
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and does not change the speed or kinetic energy of the particle; it changes only the direction of motion.

When v is perpendicular to B, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force and the particle moves in a circle; when v is parallel (or antiparallel) to B, the force is zero and the motion is a straight line; at other angles the path is a helix.

Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = direction of B, second finger = direction of conventional current (direction of motion of a positive charge), thumb = direction of force. For a negative charge the second finger points opposite to its velocity.
Positive and negative charges of the same velocity are deflected in opposite directions.
Velocity selector: in perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, a particle passes undeflected when qE = qvB, so only particles of speed v = E/B emerge.
A charge moving perpendicular to B moves in a circle: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity.
Magnetic force on a moving charge · F = qvB sinθ · F = force (N); q = charge (C); v = speed (m s⁻¹); B = magnetic flux density (T); θ = angle between v and B
Force when v ⟂ B · F = qvB · Special case θ = 90°, i.e. v perpendicular to B
Circular motion in a magnetic field · qvB = mv²/r · m = mass (kg); r = radius of the circular path (m)
Radius of circular path · r = mv/qB = p/qB · p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); from qvB = mv²/r
Period of circular motion · T = 2πm/qB · T = period (s); independent of v and r
Frequency of circular motion · f = qB/2πm · f = frequency (Hz); independent of v and r
Velocity selector · v = E/B · E = electric field strength (V m⁻¹); B = flux density (T); v = speed (m s⁻¹)
Energy gained from a p.d. · qV = ½mv² · V = accelerating potential difference (V); gain in kinetic energy equals work done by the p.d.
Speed after acceleration by a p.d. · v = √2qV/m · v = speed (m s⁻¹); q = charge (C); V = p.d. (V); m = mass (kg)
Constants for electron · e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C; mₑ = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg · e = elementary charge (C); mₑ = electron mass (kg)
Calculation: state F = qvB sinθ, substitute with SI units, give the magnitude with unit and the direction (Fleming's left-hand rule) where asked.
For circular motion write "magnetic force = centripetal force, qvB = mv²/r" before deriving r = mv/qB.
State "the force is perpendicular to the velocity, hence no work is done and the speed is constant".
In a ratio question, write r ∝ m/q (same v, B) or r ∝ v/q/m and substitute the ratios directly.

Compare: in an electric field (F = qE along the field) a charge entering perpendicularly follows a parabola and its speed changes; in a magnetic field (F = qvB ⊥ v) it follows a circle and its speed is constant.
A straight conductor of length L carrying a current I in a magnetic field B experiences a force F = BIL sinθ, perpendicular to both the conductor and the field.
Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger = field B, second finger = conventional current I, thumb = force F (motion); the three are mutually perpendicular.
The force is a maximum (BIL) when the conductor is perpendicular to B and zero when the conductor is parallel to B.
The force arises because the field exerts a force on each moving charge carrier; the sum over all the carriers in the length L gives the force on the conductor.

A rectangular coil of N turns in a uniform field experiences no net force but a torque τ = NIAB sinφ, where φ is the angle between the normal to the coil and B (equivalently NIAB cosα where α is the angle between the plane of the coil and B).
The torque is a maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B and zero when the plane is perpendicular to B; this is the principle of the moving-coil meter and the d.c. motor.
Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = BIL sin θ, perpendicular to both B and I.
Force on a current-carrying wire · F = BIL sinθ · F = force (N); B = flux density (T); I = current (A); L = length of wire in the field (m); θ = angle between the wire and B
Torque on a coil · τ = NBIA sinφ · τ = torque (N m); N = number of turns; A = area of the coil (m²); φ = angle between the normal to the coil and B
Wire balanced against its weight · BIL = mg · m = mass of wire (kg); g = acceleration of free fall (m s⁻²); B perpendicular to the wire
State the formula, substitute in SI units (cm → m, g → kg) and quote the force in newtons with the direction from Fleming's left-hand rule.
Direction: name the three directions used, e.g. "B into page, I to the right, so force is up the page".
For a coil: state "net force = 0, but the two equal and opposite forces on opposite sides form a couple, giving a torque".
For a balancing question equate magnetic force and weight, then solve for B or I.
Ampère’s law: for any closed path, the sum of the products of the length elements Δl and the component of B parallel to them equals μ₀ times the current enclosed by the path, ΣB_∥Δl = μ₀I.
Right-hand grip rule (straight wire): thumb along the conventional current, fingers curl in the direction of B.
Right-hand grip rule (coil/solenoid): fingers curl in the direction of the current, thumb points along B inside the coil, i.e. towards the north-pole end.
The field of a long straight wire consists of concentric circles; B is inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance r.
The field inside a long solenoid (far from the ends) is uniform and parallel to the axis; the field outside is very small.
Superposition: the resultant field at a point is the vector sum of the fields produced by each current; fields from different wires may cancel at a neutral point.
Two coaxial coils or concentric coils with opposing currents give zero net field at the centre when their individual fields are equal in magnitude.
Magnetic fields of a long straight wire (concentric circles) and a solenoid (uniform inside).
Field of a long straight wire · B = μ₀I/2πr · B = flux density (T); I = current (A); r = perpendicular distance from the wire (m)
Field at centre of a circular coil · B = (μ₀NI)/(2r) · N = number of turns; r = radius of the coil (m); I = current (A)
Field inside a long solenoid · B = μ₀nI = (μ₀NI)/(l) · n = number of turns per metre (m⁻¹); N = total number of turns; l = length of solenoid (m)
Field of a toroid · B = (μ₀NI)/(2πr) · r = mean radius of the ring (m); N = number of turns; I = current (A)
Permeability of free space · μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹ = 1.26×10⁻⁶ H m⁻¹ · μ₀ = permeability of free space (H m⁻¹)
Quote the formula, substitute with SI units (cm → m) and give B in tesla to 3 s.f., with direction by the right-hand grip rule when asked.
For a resultant field, find the magnitude and direction of each contribution separately, then add as vectors.
For graphs of B against r (straight wire) sketch a curve of the form 1/r: steep at small r, never reaching zero.
For a solenoid always use n = N/l (turns per metre), not N.
Neutral point between two parallel wires with currents in the same direction: set (μ₀I₁)/(2πr) = μ₀I₂/(2π(d − r)) and solve for r. Example: 4 A and 3 A, so 4/r = (3)/(d − r) and r = 4d/7.
The field of one wire exerts a force on the current in the other; by Newton's third law the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever the sizes of the currents.
Parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other; wires carrying currents in opposite directions repel each other.

The ampere is that constant current which, if maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible cross-section placed one metre apart in a vacuum, produces a force of 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre of length between them.
Explanation: wire 1 produces a field B₁ = (μ₀I₁)/(2πd) at wire 2; the force on wire 2 is F = B₁I₂L, directed by Fleming's left-hand rule towards wire 1 when the currents are parallel.
The tesla is the magnetic flux density that gives a force of 1 N per metre on a conductor carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field.
Parallel currents attract; antiparallel currents repel: F/l = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd.
Force per unit length between wires · F/L = (μ₀I₁I₂)/(2πd) · F/L = force per unit length (N m⁻¹); I₁ and I₂ = currents (A); d = separation (m)
Definition check (ampere) · F/L = (4π×10⁻⁷)/(2π) = 2×10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹ · For I₁ = I₂ = 1 A and d = 1 m
Force on a length of wire · F = (μ₀I₁I₂l)/(2πd) · l = length of one wire (m); I₁ and I₂ = currents (A); d = separation (m)
Show the field of one wire at the position of the other, then F = BIL, then direction by Fleming's left-hand rule.
State the nature: "attractive" for currents in the same direction, "repulsive" for opposite directions, with the magnitude per metre.
In the definition of the ampere include all four conditions: constant current, infinite length and negligible cross-section, 1 m apart, in a vacuum; the force is 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre.
Substitute with SI units and give F/L in N m⁻¹ to 3 s.f.; if a length l is given, multiply by l.

Rectangular loop beside a long wire: the forces on the two sides perpendicular to the wire cancel; the side nearer the wire is in a stronger field (B = μ₀I/2πr), so the net force is towards the wire when the nearer side carries current in the same direction as the wire.
Specific charge of the electron is the ratio of its charge to its mass, e/m (C kg⁻¹).
Thomson's method: electrons are accelerated and pass through crossed electric and magnetic fields; the fields are adjusted so that the beam is undeflected, so that eE = evB, giving v = E/B.
With the electric field switched off, the magnetic force makes the electrons move in a circular arc: evB = mv²/r, so e/m = v/(Br).
Alternative method: electrons accelerated through p.d. V gain kinetic energy eV = ½mv²; combined with r = mv/eB this gives e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
The experiment determines the ratio e/m only; the charge e must be found independently (Millikan's oil-drop experiment) to find m.
The ratio e/m for cathode rays is the same for all cathode materials, showing that electrons are a universal constituent of matter.
Crossed electric and magnetic fields: only electrons with v = E/B pass straight through.
Balanced fields (velocity) · eE = evB; v = E/B · e = electron charge (C); E = electric field strength (V m⁻¹); B = flux density (T); v = speed (m s⁻¹)
Magnetic deflection · r = mv/eB; e/m = v/rB · r = radius of circular path (m); m = electron mass (kg)
Accelerating p.d. · eV = ½mv²; v = √2eV/m · V = accelerating p.d. (V)
Combined expression for e/m · e/m = 2V/(B²r²) · e/m = specific charge of the electron (C kg⁻¹)
Accepted value of e/m · e/m = 1.76×10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ · Accepted value of the specific charge (C kg⁻¹)
Explain the first step: "balance electric and magnetic forces so that the beam is undeflected, hence v = E/B"; this gives the speed independently of e/m.
Describe the second step: "remove the electric field; the beam moves in a circle of radius r; magnetic force provides centripetal force".
For calculations write e/m = 2V/(B²r²), substitute with SI units and give the answer to 3 s.f. in C kg⁻¹ with the order of magnitude 10¹¹.
For error analysis: e/m ∝ V/(B²r²), so a fractional error in B or r counts twice.

A short question ("derive e/m") needs a complete answer: name the two parts (speed selector and deflection chamber), state the condition used in each (eE = evB, or eV = ½mv²; then evB = mv²/r), and combine.

Hall effect is the production of a potential difference (Hall voltage) across a current-carrying conductor or semiconductor placed in a magnetic field, the potential difference being perpendicular to both the current and the field.

Hall voltage is the transverse potential difference produced across a current-carrying conductor when a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the current, as the drifting charge carriers are deflected by the magnetic force.
Explanation: the magnetic force deflects the moving charge carriers to one side of the slab; the accumulated charge sets up a transverse electric field E_H.
The Hall voltage reaches a steady value when the electric force on a carrier balances the magnetic force: eE_H = evB.

The sign of the Hall voltage identifies the sign of the charge carriers: with the same current direction and field direction, electrons and holes are deflected to the same side but give opposite polarity across the slab (use Fleming's left-hand rule with conventional current).
In a semiconductor the carrier density n is much lower than in a metal, so V_H is much larger.
Application: a Hall probe measures B because V_H ∝ B at constant current; it is made from a thin semiconductor slab for a large V_H.
Hall effect: carriers pushed to one face set up the Hall voltage across d.

A steady current in one coil produces no current in a second coil. A current is induced only at the moment the first current is switched on or off.
Moving a magnet towards a coil induces a current; moving it away induces a current in the opposite direction; no current flows when the magnet and coil are at rest relative to each other.
The induced current is larger when the magnet moves faster, when the coil has more turns and when the magnet is stronger.

If the coil is part of a closed circuit of resistance R, the induced current is I = |ε|/R.

Lenz's law follows from the conservation of energy: if the induced current helped the change, energy would be created from nothing. Work must be done against the opposing force, and this work becomes electrical energy.

Motor and dynamo: the same machine

An electric motor is a coil in a magnetic field. A current in the coil makes forces BIl on its two long sides, one up and one down, which turn the coil (Chapter 17). A split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the coil keeps turning the same way.
Motor and dynamo: the same machine

A dynamo (like a bicycle dynamo) is the same machine used the other way round: you turn the coil, the flux through it changes, and an e.m.f. ε = NBAω sin ωt is induced. With slip rings it gives a.c.; with a commutator the output is always in one direction (d.c.).
Motor and dynamo: the same machine

In a working motor the turning coil also acts as a dynamo: it induces a back e.m.f. that opposes the supply (Lenz's law), which is why a motor takes a large current when it starts and a smaller one at full speed.
Motor and dynamo: the same machine

As a motor: switch on the current and watch the forces BIl on the two long sides turn the coil, with the commutator swapping the current every half turn. As a dynamo: turn the handle faster or slower and see the lamp and the e.m.f. graph; switch between slip rings (a.c.) and a commutator (d.c.).
Self inductionthe production of an induced e.m.f. in a coil because of a change of the current in the same coil.
Figure 18.8: the coil's own changing field changes the flux linking it.
The current in the coil produces a field and a flux through the coil itself. When the current changes, the flux changes and an e.m.f. is induced (a back e.m.f.).

By Lenz's law it opposes the change: while the current is rising the induced e.m.f. opposes the current; while it is falling the induced e.m.f. acts in the direction of the current, trying to keep it flowing.
A coil used for its self-inductance is called an inductor.
Self-inductance, Lthe ratio of the self-induced e.m.f. to the rate of change of current in the coil: L = −ε/(dI/dt). Equivalently, the flux linkage per unit current, L = NΦ/I.
LI = NΦ comes from Faraday's law: −L dI/dt = −N dΦ/dt, integrated from zero current (and zero flux).
L depends on the size and shape of the coil, the number of turns and the core material; not on the current.
Figure 18.9: when the switch is closed, the back e.m.f. of an inductor makes the current rise gradually.
While the current in an inductor is rising, a back e.m.f. opposes it. The source must do work to drive charge against this e.m.f.

This work is not lost: it is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor. When the current is switched off, the energy is given back (this is why a spark can jump across a switch that breaks an inductive circuit).
Close the switch and watch the current rise gradually while the back e.m.f. falls. Open it again and the stored energy ½LI² is given back. Change L and R: a larger L/R makes the rise slower.
Mutual inductionthe production of an induced e.m.f. in one coil because of a change of current in a neighbouring coil.
The changing current in the primary coil changes the flux linking the secondary coil, so an e.m.f. is induced in the secondary. (This is what Faraday saw when he switched the current on and off.)
The transformer and the induction coil work by mutual induction.

Mutual inductance, Mthe ratio of the e.m.f. induced in one coil to the rate of change of current in the other coil: M = −εₛ/(dIₚ/dt). Equivalently, the flux linkage of the secondary per unit current in the primary.

A transformer is two coils on one iron core. An alternating current in the primary makes a changing flux in the core, which induces an e.m.f. in the secondary by mutual induction. (A steady d.c. would give no changing flux and no output.)
A real use: transformers and power lines
For an ideal transformer: Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ and, with no energy lost, VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ.
A real use: transformers and power lines

Power stations send electricity at very high voltage (132–400 kV). For the same power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current, and the heat wasted in the cables, I²R, falls with the square of the current.
A real use: transformers and power lines
Step-up transformers raise the voltage at the power station; step-down transformers near our homes bring it back to 240 V.

Weber (Wb) is the magnetic flux when a magnetic flux density of 1 T passes perpendicularly through an area of 1 m².
Magnetic flux linkage is the product of the number of turns of a coil and the magnetic flux through each turn, NΦ.
Magnetic flux density B is the magnetic flux per unit area perpendicular to the field (the number of field lines per unit normal area), unit tesla (T = Wb m⁻²).
For a non-uniform field, the flux is found by summing the normal component of B over all area elements, Φ = ∫B·dA.
Magnetic flux through a loop: Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal.

Electromagnetic induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. (and an induced current in a closed circuit) when the magnetic flux linked with a conductor changes.
Induced e.m.f. is the e.m.f. produced in a conductor when there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with it.
Lenz's law: the direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it.
Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy: work must be done against the opposing effect to produce the induced current.
Induced e.m.f. appears whenever the flux linkage changes, by changing B, A or θ, whether or not the circuit is closed; an induced current flows only in a closed circuit.
For a straight conductor moving across a uniform field, the induced e.m.f. is the product of B, the length of the conductor and the velocity perpendicular to B.
Faraday: e.m.f. ∝ rate of change of flux linkage. Lenz: the induced current opposes the change that causes it.

Self-induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. in a coil due to a change in the current in the same coil, which changes the magnetic flux linked with it.
Self-inductance L of a coil is the ratio of the magnetic flux linkage in the coil to the current flowing through it, L = NΦ/I.
Henry (H) is the self-inductance of a coil in which an e.m.f. of 1 V is induced when the current changes at the rate of 1 A s⁻¹.
Self-inductance can also be defined as the back e.m.f. induced in a coil per unit rate of change of current in the coil, L = −ε/dI/dt.
Back e.m.f. is the induced e.m.f. produced in a circuit by a change in its own current; it opposes the change in current that produces it (Lenz’s law).
By Lenz's law, the self-induced e.m.f. always opposes the change in current: it opposes an increase in current and opposes a decrease in current.
The self-induced e.m.f. is large when the current is switched off very quickly, since dI/dt is large; this explains the spark across the switch contacts.
In an L–R circuit the back e.m.f. makes the current grow gradually towards ε/R.

The energy stored in an inductor is the work done against the self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current; it is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor.
The energy is released when the current decreases, as the self-induced e.m.f. then maintains the current for a short time.
The energy stored per unit volume of a magnetic field is the energy density, u = B²/2μ₀.
Energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor, not lost; in an ideal inductor there is no energy dissipation.
Energy stored in an inductor rises with the square of the current.

Mutual induction is the production of an induced e.m.f. in one coil due to a change in the current in a neighbouring coil, which changes the magnetic flux linked with the first coil.
Mutual inductance M is the ratio of the magnetic flux linkage in one coil to the current in the other coil that produces the flux, M = (N₂Φ₂₁)/(I₁).

Mutual induction: a changing current in one coil induces an e.m.f. in a nearby coil.

Inductive reactance X_L is the opposition of an inductor to alternating current, given by the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the inductor to the r.m.s. (or peak) current through it.
In a pure inductor, the current lags the applied voltage by 90° (π/2 rad).
The mean power dissipated in a pure inductor is zero over one complete cycle, because energy is stored in the magnetic field and returned to the source alternately.
At very high frequency, the inductor opposes the current strongly; for direct current (f = 0), X_L = 0 and the inductor offers no opposition (apart from its resistance).
Pure inductor: the current lags the voltage by 90° (X_L = ωL); mean power is zero.
Inductive reactance · X_L = ωL = 2πfL · X_L = inductive reactance (Ω); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); L = inductance (H)

X_L is directly proportional to f: a graph of X_L against f is a straight line through the origin with gradient 2πL.
For a calculation, state X_L = 2πfL, convert L to henry (mH → ×10⁻³), substitute and give the answer in Ω; then use I = V/X_L with r.m.s. values.

To explain why the mean power is zero: energy is stored in the magnetic field in one quarter-cycle and returned to the source in the next, so the net energy transfer is zero.

Capacitive reactance X_C is the opposition of a capacitor to alternating current, given by the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the capacitor to the r.m.s. (or peak) current through it.
In a pure capacitor, the current leads the applied voltage by 90° (π/2 rad).
The mean power dissipated in a pure capacitor is zero over one complete cycle, because energy is stored in the electric field and returned to the source alternately.
A capacitor blocks direct current (X_C → as f → 0) and passes high-frequency alternating current more easily (X_C → 0 as f → ).
Pure capacitor: the current leads the voltage by 90° (X_C = 1/ωC); mean power is zero.

Impedance Z is the total opposition of an a.c. circuit to the alternating current; it is the ratio of the r.m.s. (or peak) voltage across the circuit to the r.m.s. (or peak) current in it.
In a series R-L circuit, the voltage leads the current by a phase angle φ; in a series R-C circuit, the current leads the voltage by φ, where 0° < φ < 90°.
Power factor is the ratio of the mean power dissipated to the product of V_rms and I_rms, equal to cosφ = R/Z.
The mean power is dissipated only in the resistance; the inductor and capacitor dissipate no mean power.
The voltages across R and L (or C) are 90° out of phase, so the supply voltage is their phasor (vector) sum and not their arithmetic sum.
Series R–L circuit phasor diagram: V² = V_R² + V_L² and tan φ = X_L/R (for R–C, V_C points down).

194 definitions, laws and statements, with the key words the marking scheme looks for in bold, chapter by chapter. Taken from the notes, so it always matches them.
Simple harmonic motion is the motion of a particle whose acceleration is directly proportional to its displacement from a fixed (equilibrium) point and is always directed towards that point.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement of the particle from the equilibrium position (m).
Equilibrium position is the point at which no resultant force acts on the body performing SHM; displacement is measured from this point.
Period is the time taken for one complete oscillation; frequency is the number of complete oscillations per unit time.
Angular frequency is the rate of change of phase angle, ω = 2πf = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹).
Phase difference is the fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation is ahead of or behind another, expressed in radian or degree.

In SHM the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction to it. Velocity leads displacement by π/2 rad; acceleration is in antiphase (π rad) with displacement.
Displacement in SHM is a sinusoidal function of time; for a particle starting from the equilibrium position, x = A sin ωt.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, v = dx/dt, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt = −ω²x.
The speed at displacement x is given by v = ±ω√A² − x²; the speed is zero at x = ±A and maximum at x = 0.
The period of SHM is independent of the amplitude.
Total energy of a particle in undamped SHM is constant and is equal to its maximum kinetic energy (at the equilibrium position) or its maximum potential energy (at the extreme positions).
Kinetic energy is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; potential energy is zero at x = 0 and maximum at x = ±A.
Energy is continuously interchanged between kinetic and potential forms with the total remaining constant when there is no damping.
The total energy is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude.
A mass–spring system performs SHM because the restoring force on the mass is directly proportional to its extension and is directed towards the equilibrium position (Hooke's law, F = −kx).
A simple pendulum performs SHM only for small angular displacement (sin θ ≈ θ in radian, up to about 10°); the restoring force along the arc is mg sin θ ≈ mgθ.
The period of a simple pendulum is independent of the mass of the bob and of the amplitude (for small angles).
The period of a mass–spring system is independent of the amplitude and, for a vertical spring, of g.
Damped oscillation is an oscillation in which the amplitude decreases with time because energy is dissipated (as heat) by resistive forces such as air resistance or friction.

Light (under) damping: the system oscillates with amplitude decreasing exponentially with time; the period is slightly longer than that of the free oscillation (almost unchanged when the damping is light).
Critical damping: the system returns to the equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillating.
Heavy (over) damping: the system returns to the equilibrium position slowly without oscillating.
Explain damping: the resistive force does negative work on the oscillator, so the total mechanical energy decreases and the amplitude decreases.

Free oscillation is the oscillation of a system without any external force acting on it after the initial disturbance; no energy is lost, so the amplitude is constant and the system oscillates at its natural frequency.
Forced oscillation is an oscillation of a system driven by an external periodic force; it oscillates at the frequency of the driving force.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is equal to the natural frequency of the system, giving maximum amplitude of oscillation (maximum energy transfer to the system).
Effect of damping: increasing damping reduces the amplitude at resonance and makes the resonance curve broader (less sharp); the peak shifts slightly to lower frequency.
At resonance the driving force leads the displacement by π/2 rad.

A progressive (travelling) wave is a wave whose profile moves along the medium; it transfers energy from one point to another through a medium (or vacuum) by oscillations of the particles (or fields), without transferring matter.
Wavelength is the distance between two successive points that are in phase on the wave (the distance travelled by the wave in one period).
A wavefront is the locus of points which vibrate in phase.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position; period is the time for one complete oscillation of a particle.
Wave speed is the distance travelled by the wavefront per unit time.
Phase difference between two points on a progressive wave depends on their separation along the direction of travel.
In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it.
Intensity of a wave is the rate of energy transferred per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation (power per unit area), unit W m⁻².
Intensity is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude (for the same frequency and medium).
For a point source radiating uniformly in all directions with no absorption, intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source (inverse square law).
Explain the inverse square law: the same power spreads over the surface of a sphere of area 4πr², which increases as r².
Principle of superposition: when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of the individual waves at that point.
Coherent sources are sources that emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.
Constructive interference occurs when the waves meet in phase: the path difference is nλ (n = 0, 1, 2, …), giving the maximum resultant amplitude.
Destructive interference occurs when the waves meet in antiphase: the path difference is (n + ½)λ, giving the minimum resultant amplitude.
A stable, observable interference pattern requires coherent waves of similar amplitude and the same frequency.
A standing (stationary) wave is a wave whose profile does not move; it is formed by the superposition of two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.
A node is a point of zero amplitude (permanent destructive interference); an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude.
Adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes) are separated by λ/2; a node and the adjacent antinode are separated by λ/4.

Differences from a progressive wave: a standing wave does not transfer energy along the medium; its amplitude varies with position (zero at nodes); particles between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase, and particles in adjacent segments oscillate in antiphase.
For a string fixed at both ends there is a node at each end; only wavelengths with an integral number of half-wavelengths fit on the string.

Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation; they do not need a material medium.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength.
In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in phase.
Order of the spectrum, from longest wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
Electromagnetic waves can be polarised, reflected, refracted, diffracted and show interference (properties of transverse waves).
Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves in which the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation, forming alternate regions of compression and rarefaction.
A sound wave needs a material medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum, and there is no net flow of the medium from source to listener.
The speed of sound depends on the elasticity and density of the medium: v = √B/ρ in a fluid and v = √E/ρ in a solid, so v is greater in solids than in liquids and gases.
In an ideal gas v = √γRT/M = √γp/ρ, so v is proportional to √T (T in kelvin) and independent of pressure at constant temperature.
Intensity is the rate of energy flow per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation; I = P/A and I ∝ (amplitude)².
Displacement nodes are pressure antinodes and displacement antinodes are pressure nodes; the pressure variation is π/2 out of phase with the displacement.
Standing (stationary) waves in air columns and strings are formed by the superposition of a progressive wave and its reflection, giving fixed nodes and antinodes.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals a natural frequency of the system, producing a large-amplitude oscillation.
In an open pipe there is a displacement antinode at each end, so all harmonics are present: fₙ = nv/2L.
In a closed pipe there is a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics are present: fₙ = ((2n − 1)v)/(4L).
In a stretched string fixed at both ends there is a node at each end; the wave speed on the string is v = √T/μ and fₙ = nv/2L.
The antinode at an open end lies slightly beyond the pipe; this end correction makes the effective length of the air column larger than the physical length.
Intensity level (β) is a logarithmic measure of the intensity of a sound relative to the threshold of hearing: β = 10 log₁₀I/I₀, measured in decibels (dB).
The threshold of hearing I₀ = 1.0×10⁻¹² W m⁻² is the minimum intensity audible at about 1 kHz.
A difference of 10 dB corresponds to a ratio of intensities of 10; a difference of about 3 dB corresponds to a ratio of 2.
Intensity levels in dB cannot be added directly; the intensities of incoherent sources add, and the total is then converted to dB.
For a point source the intensity obeys the inverse square law, I ∝ 1/r², because the same power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr².
Beats are the periodic variations in intensity (loudness) caused by the superposition of two sound waves of slightly different frequencies.
Beats are produced because the two waves alternate between being in phase (constructive interference, loud) and in antiphase (destructive interference, soft).
The beat frequency is the number of loud (or soft) sounds heard per second and equals the magnitude of the difference between the two frequencies.
The frequency of the resultant sound is the mean of the two frequencies, and its amplitude varies at the beat frequency.
Beats can be used to compare an unknown frequency with a standard; loading or filing one source changes the beat frequency in a predictable way.
The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency of a wave due to relative motion between the source and the observer.
When a source moves towards a stationary observer, the wavelength is shortened and the observed frequency is higher; when it moves away, the wavelength is lengthened and the frequency is lower.
When an observer moves towards a stationary source, more wavefronts are intercepted per second, so the observed frequency is higher; moving away gives a lower frequency.
Speeds are taken relative to the air (medium); the speed of sound in air is unchanged by the motion of source or observer.
The Doppler shift of waves reflected from a moving object is used in radar speed guns and in medical blood-flow measurement.

Sign convention used throughout (real-is-positive): distances of real objects and real images are positive; virtual images (behind the mirror) have negative v; f and R are positive for a concave mirror and negative for a convex mirror.
The centre of curvature C is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; the radius of curvature r is the radius of that sphere.
The pole P is the centre of the reflecting surface of the mirror; the aperture is the size (area) of the reflecting surface.
The principal axis is the line through the pole and the centre of curvature; it is normal to the mirror at its pole.
The principal focus of a concave mirror is the point on the principal axis through which rays parallel and close to the axis converge after reflection.
The focal length is the distance from the pole to the principal focus; f = R/2 for a spherical mirror of small aperture, where R is the radius of curvature.
Linear magnification is the ratio of the image height to the object height, m = h_i/hₒ = −v/u; m is negative for an inverted (real) image and positive for an upright (virtual) image.
A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image for u > f and a virtual, upright, magnified image for u < f; a convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.

Sign convention (real-is-positive): u is positive for a real object in front of the surface; v is positive for a real image formed on the side where light emerges, negative for a virtual image on the object side; R is positive when the centre of curvature lies on the outgoing (emerging) side, i.e. a surface convex towards the incident light.
Refraction at a spherical surface obeys Snell's law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r at each point; for paraxial rays this leads to the surface equation below.
Apparent depth: an object in a denser medium appears closer to the surface when viewed normally, because rays bend away from the normal on leaving it.
A plane surface has R → , so the term (n₂ − n₁)/(R) vanishes; then n₁/u + n₂/v = 0 and v/u = −n₂/n₁.

Sign convention (real-is-positive): u positive for a real object; v positive for a real image (on the opposite side of the lens), negative for a virtual image; f positive for a converging (convex) lens and negative for a diverging (concave) lens.
The principal focus of a converging lens is the point on the axis to which rays parallel and close to the axis converge after refraction through the lens.
The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, P = 1/f, with unit dioptre (D).
Linear magnification m = h_i/hₒ = −v/u; a real image from a single lens is inverted (m negative); a virtual image is upright (m positive).
A convex lens forms a real, inverted image when u > f and a virtual, upright, magnified image when u < f (magnifying glass); a concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.
Wavefront is a line or surface joining all points of a wave that are in phase (same displacement and same direction of motion).

Huygens's principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront after a short time t is the envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave into the geometrical shadow when it passes the edge of an obstacle or through a gap; the points at the edge act as sources of secondary wavelets that spread into the shadow region.

Reflection and refraction: construction with secondary wavelets gives the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and Snell's law; on refraction the frequency is unchanged while the speed and wavelength change.
Interference is the superposition of two or more coherent waves, producing a pattern of reinforcement (maxima) and cancellation (minima).
Coherent sources are sources that emit waves of the same frequency (wavelength) with a constant phase difference.

Optical path between two points in a medium is the distance in vacuum that contains the same number of wavelengths as the medium between the two points, for light of the same frequency; optical path = nd, where n is the refractive index and d the actual distance.
Constructive interference occurs when the waves meet in phase (path difference = nλ, n = 0, 1, 2, …); destructive interference occurs when they meet in antiphase (path difference = (n + ½)λ).
Two separate light bulbs do not give a stable interference pattern because the phase relationship of their light changes randomly and rapidly, so they are not coherent.

On reflection from a medium of higher refractive index (denser medium) the wave undergoes a phase change of π (equivalent to a path change of λ/2); there is no phase change on reflection at a less dense medium.

Young's double-slit experiment: light from a single narrow slit (or a laser) illuminates two narrow slits S₁ and S₂ which act as coherent sources; the overlapping diffracted waves produce alternate bright and dark fringes on a screen.
The bright fringe is formed where the path difference S₂P − S₁P = nλ; the dark fringe where S₂P − S₁P = (n + ½)λ.
Fringes are equally spaced and of nearly equal brightness near the centre; the central fringe (n = 0) is bright because the path difference is zero.
With white light, the central fringe is white and the other fringes are coloured (violet nearest the centre, red furthest) since fringe spacing ∝ λ.

Thin-film interference is the interference between the light reflected from the top surface and the light reflected from the bottom surface of the film; the two beams are coherent because they originate from the same incident wave.
A phase change of π occurs on reflection when the light is reflected from a medium of higher refractive index; there is no phase change on reflection from a medium of lower refractive index.
Colours of a thin film in white light: the film thickness varies, so different wavelengths satisfy the condition for constructive interference at different places, giving coloured bands.

Air wedge: the air layer between two glass plates in contact at one edge; the fringes are straight, parallel and equally spaced, and the fringe at the line of contact is dark because of the π phase change at one reflection only.
Non-reflective coating: a thin film of refractive index between those of air and glass; the reflected beams from the two surfaces interfere destructively so that reflection is reduced.
Diffraction is the spreading of waves when they pass through a gap or round an obstacle; it is most marked when the width of the gap is comparable with the wavelength.
A single-slit diffraction pattern has a wide, bright central maximum with weaker secondary maxima on both sides; the intensity of the secondary maxima falls rapidly.
The pattern arises from interference between the secondary wavelets from different points across the width of the slit.
The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum; the minima occur where the path difference between the two edges of the slit is a whole number of wavelengths.

Diffraction grating is an optical device with a large number of equally spaced parallel slits (lines) of very narrow width; the diffracted beams interfere to produce sharp, bright maxima at definite angles.
Grating spacing d is the distance between the centres of adjacent slits; d = 1/N, where N is the number of lines per unit length.
The maxima occur where the path difference between light from adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths.
With white light, the zero-order maximum is white and each higher order is a spectrum with violet nearest and red furthest from the centre; the higher orders may overlap.
Increasing the number of lines illuminated makes the maxima sharper and brighter; the angular positions of the maxima depend on d and λ only.
Plane-polarised (linearly polarised) light is light in which the electric field vibrations are in one plane only, perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

Unpolarised light is light whose electric field vibrations occur in all planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation; it can be resolved into two mutually perpendicular components of equal intensity, both perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Plane of polarisation is the plane containing the electric field vibrations of the wave and the direction of propagation.
Only transverse waves can be polarised; the polarisation of light shows that light is a transverse wave, whereas sound (a longitudinal wave) cannot be polarised.
Polariser produces plane-polarised light from unpolarised light; analyser is a second polariser used to detect the plane of polarisation.

Malus's law: the intensity of plane-polarised light transmitted through an analyser is proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between the plane of polarisation of the light and the transmission axis of the analyser.

Brewster's law: when light is incident at the polarising angle θ_B, the reflected light is completely plane-polarised (vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence) and the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other.
Unpolarised light passing through an ideal polariser is reduced to half of the incident intensity.
Optical fibre is a thin strand of glass or plastic consisting of a core surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index; light is guided along the core by total internal reflection.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
Critical angle θ_c is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is 90°.
Conditions for guiding: n_core > n_cladding and the angle of incidence at the core–cladding boundary greater than θ_c.
Attenuation is the loss of power as the signal travels along the fibre, caused by absorption and scattering in the glass.
Modal dispersion is the spreading (broadening) of a pulse because rays following different paths take different times; it is reduced in a very narrow core (single-mode) fibre or a graded-index fibre.
Photon is a quantum (packet) of electromagnetic radiation of energy E = hf; it is a neutral particle with zero rest mass that travels at the speed of light.
Photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency falls on it.
Compton effect is the scattering of X-ray photons by electrons in atoms; the scattered photon has a longer wavelength (lower energy) than the incident photon, showing that a photon carries momentum.
Work function φ is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal; threshold frequency f₀ is the minimum frequency for emission, f₀ = φ/h.
Stopping potential Vₛ is the minimum reverse potential difference that reduces the photocurrent to zero; eVₛ = Kₘₐₓ.
Einstein's photoelectric equation: hf = φ + Kₘₐₓ, an electron absorbs one photon whose energy is shared between the work function and the kinetic energy.
Observations that wave theory cannot explain: a threshold frequency exists; Kₘₐₓ is independent of intensity and depends on frequency; emission is instantaneous.
Wave-particle duality: radiation and matter exhibit both wave properties (diffraction, interference) and particle properties (photoelectric effect, photon momentum) depending on the experiment.
de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p.
Wave nature of electrons is shown by electron diffraction through a thin crystal or graphite film (Davisson–Germer experiment): a ring (diffraction) pattern is formed.
Particle nature of light is shown by the photoelectric effect; wave nature of light by diffraction and interference.
The wave behaviour of macroscopic objects is not observed because the de Broglie wavelength is far too small compared with any obstacle or gap.

Line spectrum consists of discrete bright lines (emission) or dark lines (absorption) of definite wavelengths, characteristic of the element; it shows that electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels.

Bohr's postulates: electrons move in certain stable orbits without radiating energy (stationary states); the angular momentum of an orbiting electron is quantised, mvr = nh/2π; radiation is emitted or absorbed only when an electron makes a transition between two levels, hf = E_i − E_f.
Energy level is the energy of an electron in an allowed orbit in the atom.
Ground state is the state in which the electron in the atom has the lowest energy (n = 1); an excited state is any state with energy higher than the ground state.
Excitation energy is the energy needed to raise an electron from the ground state to an excited state.
Ionisation energy is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the ground state of an atom so that it is completely detached from the atom (n = ); for hydrogen it is 13.6 eV.
Spectral series of hydrogen: Lyman (transitions to n = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (to n = 2, visible), Paschen (to n = 3, infrared).
Laser action: stimulated emission produces photons identical in phase, frequency and direction to the stimulating photon; population inversion is needed for light amplification.
X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁹ m), produced when fast electrons are suddenly stopped by a metal target.

Continuous spectrum arises from the deceleration of electrons in the target (bremsstrahlung); it has a sharp cut-off at the minimum wavelength λ_min, corresponding to the whole kinetic energy of an electron being converted to a single photon.

Characteristic spectrum consists of sharp lines produced when an incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron of the target atom and an outer electron falls to fill the vacancy; the lines are characteristic of the target material.
Bragg's law: constructive interference occurs for X-rays reflected from successive crystal planes when the path difference 2d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths.
Glancing angle θ is the angle between the incident X-ray beam and the atomic (crystal) plane.
Intensity of the X-ray beam depends on the tube current; the penetrating power (hardness) depends on the accelerating voltage.
Nanoscience is the study of materials and structures with at least one dimension of the order of 1 nm to 100 nm.
The surface-area-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles is very large, so a large proportion of atoms lie at the surface, which gives a high chemical reactivity and catalytic activity.

Scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) uses the quantum-mechanical tunnelling current between a sharp conducting tip and the surface; the current depends very sensitively (exponentially) on the tip–surface separation, so atoms can be imaged.
Examples: carbon nanotubes (high strength, electrical conduction), graphene, nanoparticles in sunscreens and catalysts.
The proton (atomic) number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus; the nucleon (mass) number A is the total number of protons and neutrons; the number of neutrons N = A − Z.
Isotopes are nuclides of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A).
A nuclide is a particular species of nucleus with a specified proton number Z and nucleon number A.
The unified atomic mass unit (u) is one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg ≡ 931.5 MeV.
The mass defect is the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
The binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons; B = Δmc².

The binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons. It is a measure of nuclear stability: a nucleus with a greater binding energy per nucleon is more stable; the curve rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 MeV near ⁵⁶Fe (A ≈ 56) and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.
The nuclear radius R = R₀A^1/3, so the nuclear density is the same for all nuclei (about 2×10¹⁷ kg m⁻³).
Radioactive decay is the spontaneous and random disintegration of an unstable nucleus with the emission of α, β or γ radiation.

Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous. Random: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, and every nucleus has the same probability of decay per unit time. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external physical conditions such as temperature and pressure.
The activity A is the rate of decay of the nuclei, A = −dN/dt = λN, measured in becquerel (Bq; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second).
The decay constant λ is the probability of decay per unit time of a nucleus.
The half-life t½ is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to fall to half of its initial value.
α emission reduces A by 4 and Z by 2; β⁻ emission raises Z by 1 with A unchanged; γ emission changes neither A nor Z.
In a nuclear reaction, mass number, charge (atomic number), energy and momentum are conserved; rest mass is not conserved.
The Q-value of a reaction is the energy released (Q > 0) or absorbed (Q < 0), Q = (total mass of reactants − total mass of products)c².

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (e.g. ²³⁵U, after absorbing a neutron) into two lighter nuclei with the release of energy and neutrons; each fission of ²³⁵U releases about 200 MeV.
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus with the release of energy; it requires a very high temperature to overcome electrostatic repulsion.
Energy is released in fission and fusion because the products have a greater binding energy per nucleon, so their total mass is less than that of the reactants.
A chain reaction is sustained when, on average, at least one of the secondary neutrons from each fission causes another fission.

A thermal neutron is a slow neutron whose kinetic energy is about the same as the thermal energy of particles at room temperature (about 0.025 eV); thermal neutrons are the most likely to cause fission of ²³⁵U.

A thermonuclear reaction is a fusion reaction that occurs when the temperature of the light nuclei is raised to about 10⁸ K, so that they collide with enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion and fuse.

Work done by a gas is the area under the p–V graph (W = ∫p dV), and Q = ΔU + W. Constant volume: W = 0. Constant pressure: W = pΔV = nRΔT. Isothermal: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), ΔU = 0. Adiabatic: W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(γ − 1), Q = 0. With worked examples.

Heat is the energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Radiation transfers it as electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared) and needs no medium. Power radiated P = eσAT⁴; Wien’s law λmax T = b; a good absorber is a good emitter; net rate P_net = eσA(T₀⁴ − Tₛ⁴).

The Sun (≈ 5800 K) emits short-wavelength radiation that warms the Earth’s surface. The cooler surface (≈ 288 K) emits long-wavelength infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit, partly back to the surface. More greenhouse gases from human activities give the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.

Doppler effect (four cases) : f′ = (f(v ± uₒ))/(v ∓ uₛ)
Stationary source of frequency f; speed of sound v; wavelength λ = v/f.
(a) Observer moves towards the source at uₒ: the wavelength is unchanged, but the sound passes the observer at relative speed v + uₒ, so f′ = (v + uₒ)/(λ) = (f(v + uₒ))/(v).
(b) Observer moves away from the source: relative speed v − uₒ, so f′ = (f(v − uₒ))/(v).

(c) Source moves towards the observer at uₛ: in one period 1/f the wave moves v/f while the source moves uₛ/f, so the wavelength in front is shortened to λ′ = (v − uₛ)/(f). The speed of sound is unchanged: f′ = v/λ′ = (fv)/(v − uₛ).
(d) Source moves away from the observer: λ′ = (v + uₛ)/(f), so f′ = (fv)/(v + uₛ).
Both moving: combine the two effects, f′ = (f(v ± uₒ))/(v ∓ uₛ) (upper signs when approaching).
Observer moving: the wavelength stays the same, the relative speed changes. Source moving: the wavelength changes, the speed of sound stays the same.

Oscillation (periodic motion)is the back-and-forth motion of an object about a fixed point.

The simplest oscillation is a mass on a spring sliding on a smooth horizontal surface (Figure 20.1). We assume the spring is light (its mass is ignored) and there is no friction.
Figure 20.1: (a) spring stretched, the force acts to the left; (b) at the equilibrium position, F = 0; (c) spring compressed, the force acts to the right.
The spring has a natural length at which it exerts no force on the mass. The position of the mass at this point is the equilibrium position.
If the mass is pulled to the right (spring stretched) or pushed to the left (spring compressed), the spring exerts a force that acts to return it to equilibrium. This is the restoring force.
At x = 0 the restoring force is zero, but the mass keeps moving past O because of its inertia.
The restoring force is always directed towards the equilibrium position.
