Dampingis the decrease in amplitude of an oscillation caused by dissipative forces such as friction and air resistance.
Part of the energy of the system is used to overcome these resistive forces, and is lost as heat.
So the amplitude does not stay constant: it decreases gradually (exponentially) until the oscillation stops. Since E ∝ A², the energy decreases too.
A damped oscillation is therefore not perfect SHM.
Figure 20.7: under damping: the oscillation continues but the amplitude decreases with time.
Figure 20.8: displacement against time for the three types of damping, each released from the same displacement.

Under damping (light damping) · The system oscillates, with the amplitude decreasing with time until it becomes zero. It takes a long time to die away. · a mass oscillating in air; a plucked guitar string
Critical damping · The system does not oscillate. It returns to the equilibrium position in the shortest possible time. · the shock absorbers of a car
Over damping (heavy damping) · The system does not oscillate, but it takes a long time to return to equilibrium. · a car fuel gauge; bathroom scales; a heavy door closer

Increase the damping from none to under, critical and over damping. Watch the mass, the displacement–time graph and the energy. Critical damping brings the mass back to O fastest without overshooting.
The system is displaced and released, then left alone: no driving force. · A periodic external force (the driving force) acts on the system continuously.
It oscillates at its own natural frequency f₀. · After a short time, it oscillates at the driving (forcing) frequency f, not at f₀.
Its amplitude depends only on the energy given at the start (it is damped gradually if there is resistance). · Its amplitude depends on how close f is to f₀.
Natural frequencyis the frequency at which a system oscillates when there is no driving force and no damping. For a simple pendulum, f₀ = 1/2π√g/l.
Figure 20.9: the driver pendulum D and pendulums X, Y, Z hang from the same string. Only Y has the same length as D.
X, Y and Z are at rest at first. D is set swinging.
Energy is passed along the string, so X, Y and Z start to oscillate (forced oscillation), all at the frequency of D.
Y, with the same length (and so the same natural frequency) as D, oscillates with the largest amplitude. Y is in resonance.

Resonanceoccurs when the frequency of the driving force is equal to the natural frequency of the system. The system then absorbs energy from the driving force most efficiently, and the amplitude of oscillation is maximum.
Figure 20.10: amplitude of the forced oscillation against driving frequency for different amounts of damping.
Damping absorbs energy and reduces the effect of resonance.
As the damping increases, the amplitude at resonance decreases and the resonance peak becomes broader (flatter).
With heavier damping, the peak also moves slightly below f₀.

Slowly change the driving frequency and watch the amplitude of the driven mass. The amplitude is largest when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency. Then increase the damping and see the peak fall and become broader.
1940, Washington State, USA: the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge collapsed about four months after opening. A strong wind drove the bridge into large oscillations.
1850, Angers, France: more than 200 soldiers died when a bridge they were marching over collapsed. This is why soldiers break step when they march across a bridge.
A singer can shatter a wine glass with a note at its natural frequency.
The tuning circuit of a radio or TV resonates at the frequency of the chosen station.
Wind instruments produce sound by making the air column inside resonate.
Microwave ovens heat food because water molecules absorb energy from the microwaves.

A mass–spring system performs SHM because the restoring force on the mass is directly proportional to its extension and is directed towards the equilibrium position (Hooke's law, F = −kx).
A simple pendulum performs SHM only for small angular displacement (sin θ ≈ θ in radian, up to about 10°); the restoring force along the arc is mg sin θ ≈ mgθ.
The period of a simple pendulum is independent of the mass of the bob and of the amplitude (for small angles).
The period of a mass–spring system is independent of the amplitude and, for a vertical spring, of g.

Damped oscillation is an oscillation in which the amplitude decreases with time because energy is dissipated (as heat) by resistive forces such as air resistance or friction.

Light (under) damping: the system oscillates with amplitude decreasing exponentially with time; the period is slightly longer than that of the free oscillation (almost unchanged when the damping is light).
Critical damping: the system returns to the equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillating.
Heavy (over) damping: the system returns to the equilibrium position slowly without oscillating.
Explain damping: the resistive force does negative work on the oscillator, so the total mechanical energy decreases and the amplitude decreases.
Damping: light damping decays slowly; critical damping returns fastest without oscillating; heavy damping returns slowly.
Amplitude decay · A = A₀e^−bt · A₀ = initial amplitude (m); b = damping constant (s⁻¹); t = time (s)
Energy decay · E ∝ A²; E = E₀e^−2bt · E = energy (J); E₀ = initial energy (J); b = damping constant (s⁻¹); t = time (s)
Exponential decay of amplitude · A₂/A₁ = A₁/A₀ · For equal time intervals the amplitude falls by the same factor (exponential decay); A₀, A₁, A₂ = amplitudes at successive equal intervals (m)
Half-life of amplitude · t½ = (ln 2)/(b) · t½ = half-life of amplitude (s); b = damping constant (s⁻¹)
For a displacement–time graph of light damping, sketch oscillations whose peaks lie on an exponentially decaying envelope; label both axes.
For critical and heavy damping, sketch a curve that falls to zero without crossing the time axis; critical damping reaches zero faster than heavy damping.
Always state the energy change: mechanical energy is converted to thermal energy by the resistive force.
Give a use of each type: critical damping in a car suspension, a galvanometer and door closers.

When asked to compare free, light, critical and heavy damping on one displacement–time graph, start every curve from the amplitude (x = A at t = 0). The comparison refers to an experiment in which the system is pulled to its amplitude and released. Free oscillation: constant amplitude and period; light damping: decaying amplitude; critical damping: returns to zero fastest without crossing; heavy damping: returns slow…

Free oscillation is the oscillation of a system without any external force acting on it after the initial disturbance; no energy is lost, so the amplitude is constant and the system oscillates at its natural frequency.
Forced oscillation is an oscillation of a system driven by an external periodic force; it oscillates at the frequency of the driving force.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is equal to the natural frequency of the system, giving maximum amplitude of oscillation (maximum energy transfer to the system).
Effect of damping: increasing damping reduces the amplitude at resonance and makes the resonance curve broader (less sharp); the peak shifts slightly to lower frequency.
At resonance the driving force leads the displacement by π/2 rad.
Resonance: amplitude is largest when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency; damping lowers and broadens the peak.
Natural frequency, mass–spring · f₀ = 1/2π√k/m · f₀ = natural frequency (Hz); k = force constant (N m⁻¹); m = mass (kg)
Natural frequency, simple pendulum · f₀ = 1/2π√g/L · f₀ = natural frequency (Hz); g = acceleration of free fall (m s⁻²); L = length (m)
Resonance condition · f_driving = f₀ · f_driving = frequency of the driving force (Hz); f₀ = natural frequency (Hz)
Graph: amplitude against driving frequency, with a peak at f₀.
For the resonance graph, label axes (amplitude against driving frequency), draw a peak at f₀ and show a second curve for heavier damping which is lower and broader.
Explain resonance in two points: driving frequency equals natural frequency; energy transferred to the system at the maximum rate, so the amplitude is maximum.
Give examples with a consequence: collapse of a bridge or a building in an earthquake; useful: tuning of a radio circuit, microwave oven.
Calculation: find f₀ = 1/2π√k/m and state that resonance occurs at this driving frequency.

The energy spreads out over the surface of a sphere of area 4πr², so I = (P)/(4πr²).
The intensity therefore decreases with distance: I ∝ 1/r² (the inverse square law).

Principle of superpositionstates that when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement at that point is the vector sum of the displacements due to each individual wave.
Figure 21.6: two pulses meeting. (a) Displacements in the same direction add. (b) Displacements in opposite directions partly cancel. After meeting, each pulse continues unchanged.
The waves interfere with each other only while they overlap.
Constructive interference: the displacements are in the same direction, giving a larger resultant.
Destructive interference: the displacements are in opposite directions, giving a smaller resultant (zero if they are equal and opposite).

Send two pulses towards each other, on the same side or on opposite sides. Pause while they overlap: the resultant (green) is the sum of the two displacements at every point. After they pass, each pulse is unchanged.
A small microphone on the outside of each ear cup picks up the noise around you (an aeroplane engine, a bus, an air-conditioner).
The electronics produce an "anti-noise" wave with the same amplitude but opposite phase (a phase difference of π), and the speaker plays it into your ear.
At your ear the two waves superpose: y = y_noise + y_anti ≈ 0. This is destructive interference.
It works best for steady, low-frequency sounds. For high frequencies even a tiny delay in the electronics is a large fraction of a period, so the anti-noise is no longer in antiphase.

Switch the noise cancelling on and off and compare the sound reaching the ear (green). Then add a delay in the electronics or change the noise frequency: the cancellation gets worse once the phase difference moves away from π. Switch on the sound to hear it (use earphones for the low hum).
Standing (stationary) waveis formed by the superposition of two progressive waves of the same amplitude and frequency, travelling at the same speed in opposite directions.
A wave travelling along a string is reflected at the end. The incident and reflected waves travel in opposite directions and superpose to form a standing wave.
Figure 21.7: a pulse is inverted when it is reflected at a fixed end, and is not inverted at a free end.
At some points the two waves are always equal and opposite, so they always cancel: these points do not move. They are nodes (N).
Midway between the nodes, the two waves always add, giving the largest oscillation. These points are antinodes (A).
Figure 21.8: a standing wave. The profile does not move along; each point oscillates with its own amplitude.

Two identical waves travel in opposite directions (blue and orange). Their sum (green) is a standing wave: the nodes never move and the antinodes have the largest amplitude. Switch to the string to see the harmonics of a string fixed at both ends.

The wave profile does not move; energy is not transferred from one particle to the next. · The wave profile moves in the direction of propagation and energy is transferred.
There are points (nodes) that are not displaced at all. · No nodes.

Points between two successive nodes oscillate in phase, with the same frequency. · Neighbouring points are not in phase, but have the same frequency.
An electromagnetic (EM) wave is made up of an electric field and a magnetic field that vibrate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, in phase.
Figure 21.10: an electromagnetic wave travelling in the +x direction.
The electric field (red) and the magnetic field (violet) vibrate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, and reach their maxima together.
They do not need a medium: they can travel through a vacuum.
They all travel at the same speed in a vacuum, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
They carry no charge, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
They show reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation.
vibrations of electric and magnetic fields · vibrations of the particles of a medium
do not need a medium; can travel in a vacuum · need a medium; cannot travel in a vacuum
speed in a vacuum = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ · much slower (e.g. sound in air ≈ 340 m s⁻¹)
e.g. light, radio waves, X-rays · e.g. sound, water waves, waves on a string

Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?

On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9 earthquake off north-east Japan sent a tsunami onto the Tōhoku coast. The old sea walls were designed for waves of about 8 m, but the waves reached 12–15 m, poured over the walls and destroyed many of them. About 20 000 people died.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?
Japan then built nearly 400 km of new concrete sea walls along the coast, up to 14.7 m high, with deep foundations and wider bases so they do not collapse if a wave goes over the top.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?
While you watch: compare the height of the tsunami in the open ocean with its height when it reaches the coast.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?
A tsunami is a progressive wave with a very long wavelength (hundreds of kilometres). Its speed depends on the depth of the water: v = √(gd) (given).
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?
In the deep ocean it travels at about 700–900 km h⁻¹ but is often less than 1 m high. Near the coast the water becomes shallow, so the wave slows down.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?

The frequency stays the same (it is set by the source), so from v = fλ the wavelength becomes shorter. The same energy is squeezed into a shorter, slower wave, so the amplitude grows. Since I ∝ A², the wave arriving at the wall is extremely powerful.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?
The frequency is fixed by the source. The speed falls in shallow water, so λ = v/f falls. The energy is concentrated into a shorter wave, so the amplitude increases.
Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the shore?

A progressive (travelling) wave is a wave whose profile moves along the medium; it transfers energy from one point to another through a medium (or vacuum) by oscillations of the particles (or fields), without transferring matter.
Wavelength is the distance between two successive points that are in phase on the wave (the distance travelled by the wave in one period).
A wavefront is the locus of points which vibrate in phase.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position; period is the time for one complete oscillation of a particle.
Wave speed is the distance travelled by the wavefront per unit time.
Phase difference between two points on a progressive wave depends on their separation along the direction of travel.
In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it.
A progressive wave: amplitude A, wavelength λ; v = fλ.

Say that energy is transferred in the direction of wave propagation but the particles only oscillate about their equilibrium positions.

To find the phase angle φ from a displacement graph, read y at t = 0 (or x = 0): y₀ = A sin φ. For example, y₀ = 0.50A gives φ = 30° = π/6 rad.
Intensity of a wave is the rate of energy transferred per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation (power per unit area), unit W m⁻².
Intensity is directly proportional to the square of the amplitude (for the same frequency and medium).
For a point source radiating uniformly in all directions with no absorption, intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source (inverse square law).
Explain the inverse square law: the same power spreads over the surface of a sphere of area 4πr², which increases as r².
Intensity from a point source spreads over a sphere: I = P/4πr², and I ∝ amplitude².

Principle of superposition: when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of the individual waves at that point.
Coherent sources are sources that emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.

Destructive interference occurs when the waves meet in antiphase: the path difference is (n + ½)λ, giving the minimum resultant amplitude.
A stable, observable interference pattern requires coherent waves of similar amplitude and the same frequency.
Superposition: where waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.

A standing (stationary) wave is a wave whose profile does not move; it is formed by the superposition of two progressive waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions.
A node is a point of zero amplitude (permanent destructive interference); an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude.
Adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes) are separated by λ/2; a node and the adjacent antinode are separated by λ/4.

Understand what "energy is not transferred" means: a standing wave stores energy in the vibrating medium. This is why standing waves are the sources of sound (stretched strings, closed and open pipes, drums).

Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation; they do not need a material medium.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength.
In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in phase.
Order of the spectrum, from longest wavelength: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
Electromagnetic waves can be polarised, reflected, refracted, diffracted and show interference (properties of transverse waves).
Electromagnetic wave: E and B oscillate in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.

A sound wave is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel.
The source of a sound wave is a vibrating object.
The sound wave travels as a series of compressions and rarefactions of the medium.
Sound travels slowest in gases, faster in liquids and fastest in solids. In a gas the speed depends on temperature: in air, v ≈ (331 + 0.606θ) m s⁻¹, θ in °C.

When the prongs move outwards, they push the air in front of them together. The pressure rises slightly: a compression (condensation).
How a tuning fork produces sound
When the prongs move inwards, the air spreads out. The pressure falls slightly below normal: a rarefaction.

As the fork keeps vibrating, compressions and rarefactions are produced one after another and spread away from it.

Figure 22.1: (a) the air layers at one instant (C = compression, R = rarefaction); (b) displacement y of the air particles against distance x; (c) excess pressure p against distance x.

At a compression or a rarefaction, the particles have zero displacement (they pass through their equilibrium position at maximum speed). Here the pressure is maximum (compression, above pₐₜₘ) or minimum (rarefaction, below pₐₜₘ).
Where the displacement is maximum (y = ±y₀), the particles are momentarily at rest, their spacing is normal, and the excess pressure is zero.
So the pressure wave and the displacement wave are π/2 rad (a quarter cycle) out of phase: the pressure wave leads the displacement wave by π/2.

Watch the air layers. Each layer only vibrates back and forth about its own position. The compressions (dark) and rarefactions (light) move along. Compare the displacement graph with the pressure graph: they are a quarter cycle apart.
Sound is a series of compressions and rarefactions (pressure variations) that travel through the air.
Sound waves travel in air as longitudinal waves: the air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation.
The source of any sound is a vibrating object, e.g. musical instruments (guitar, violin, flute, trumpet). The vibrations are standing waves on strings or in air columns.

Guitar: each string is fixed at the bridge and at the nut, so it vibrates with nodes at both ends: f₁ = 1/2l√T/μ. Thicker strings (larger μ) give lower notes; turning the tuning peg changes the tension T.
Real instruments: the guitar and the flute

Pressing a string against a fret shortens the vibrating length. The frets are placed so that each one raises the note by a semitone; the 12th fret is halfway along the string, so the note is one octave higher (double the frequency).
Real instruments: the guitar and the flute

Flute: a pipe open at both ends (the mouth hole and the far end), so there is an antinode at each end: f₁ = v/2l. Opening a finger hole makes the air column end there, so it is shorter and the note is higher.

Blowing harder makes the flute sound its second harmonic (overblowing): the same fingering gives a note one octave higher.

Intensity of soundis the rate of energy transported per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation: I = E/tA = P/A, unit W m⁻².
For a point source radiating uniformly, A = 4πr², so I₂/I₁ = r₁²/r₂². The intensity (and so the loudness) depends on the amplitude, I ∝ A², and on the distance, I ∝ 1/r².
Threshold of hearing: the lowest intensity a normal ear can detect, I₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻².
Threshold of pain: about 1 W m⁻².
Our sense of loudness follows the logarithm of the intensity, so a logarithmic scale is used.
Intensity level of sound, βis a logarithmic measure of the intensity of a sound compared with the threshold of hearing.
Beatsare the periodic variation in amplitude (loudness) at a point, caused by the superposition of two sound waves of slightly different frequencies.
Figure 22.6: two waves of 50 Hz and 60 Hz and their sum. The loudness rises and falls 10 times per second.
Where the two waves are in phase, they interfere constructively: the amplitude is maximum and a loud sound is heard.
Where they are in antiphase, they interfere destructively: the amplitude is minimum and little or no sound is heard.
The number of times per second the loudness rises and falls is the beat frequency.
Set two frequencies that are close together. The green curve is their sum: its amplitude rises and falls at the beat frequency. Press Listen to hear the beats (use earphones or a speaker).
At first |350 − f₂| = 3, so f₂ = 347 Hz or 353 Hz. Tightening increases the tension, so f₂ increases. The beat frequency falls from 3 to 2, so f₂ moved closer to 350 Hz: it was 347 Hz (now 348 Hz).
Doppler effectis the change in the observed frequency of a wave because of the relative motion between the source and the observer.
Figure 22.7: a moving source. The wavefronts are closer together in front of the source and further apart behind it.
Source at rest: every observer hears the source frequency fₛ.
Source moving towards the observer: the wavelength reaching the observer is shorter, so the observed frequency is higher (f′ > fₛ).
Source moving away: the wavelength is longer, so the observed frequency is lower (f′ < fₛ).
Figure 22.8: the frequency heard by a stationary observer as a source approaches, passes and moves away at constant speed.
While the source approaches, the observed frequency is constant and higher than fₛ; it drops to fₛ as the source passes; it is then constant and lower while the source moves away.
The loudness does change: as the source comes closer, r decreases and I ∝ 1/r² increases. Do not confuse loudness (intensity) with pitch (frequency).
Move the source, or the observer, and watch the wavefronts. Compare the frequency heard by the observer in front of the source with the one behind it.

Moving source: each new wavefront is emitted closer to the one before, so the wavefronts bunch up ahead.
The wavelength in front decreases: λ′ = (v − vₛ) / f.
The speed of sound in air does not change with the source’s motion.
Moving observer: the wavelength is unchanged, but the waves pass the observer at relative speed v + vₒ.
So the observer meets more wavefronts per second: f′ = (v + vₒ) / λ.
Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves in which the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of propagation, forming alternate regions of compression and rarefaction.
A sound wave needs a material medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum, and there is no net flow of the medium from source to listener.
The speed of sound depends on the elasticity and density of the medium: v = √B/ρ in a fluid and v = √E/ρ in a solid, so v is greater in solids than in liquids and gases.
In an ideal gas v = √γRT/M = √γp/ρ, so v is proportional to √T (T in kelvin) and independent of pressure at constant temperature.
Intensity is the rate of energy flow per unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation; I = P/A and I ∝ (amplitude)².
Displacement nodes are pressure antinodes and displacement antinodes are pressure nodes; the pressure variation is π/2 out of phase with the displacement.
Sound: compressions (C) and rarefactions (R); pressure variation is 90° out of phase with displacement.

Explain the propagation of sound in the correct sequence: (1) the vibrating source makes the air particles move to and fro; (2) compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) are formed; (3) the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of propagation, so a longitudinal wave travels through the air. Correct points in the wrong order may score no marks. Ask yourself: "If this happens, what follows next…

On a displacement–distance graph (displacement to the right taken as positive), the point midway between a positive maximum displacement and the next negative maximum displacement is a compression: maximum pressure. Midway from a negative maximum to a positive maximum is a rarefaction: minimum pressure. Work this out before the exam; it has been asked more than once.
Standing (stationary) waves in air columns and strings are formed by the superposition of a progressive wave and its reflection, giving fixed nodes and antinodes.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals a natural frequency of the system, producing a large-amplitude oscillation.
In an open pipe there is a displacement antinode at each end, so all harmonics are present: fₙ = nv/2L.
In a closed pipe there is a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics are present: fₙ = ((2n − 1)v)/(4L).
In a stretched string fixed at both ends there is a node at each end; the wave speed on the string is v = √T/μ and fₙ = nv/2L.
The antinode at an open end lies slightly beyond the pipe; this end correction makes the effective length of the air column larger than the physical length.
Stationary waves on a string (all harmonics) and in pipes: open pipes have all harmonics, closed pipes only odd ones.

Intensity level (β) is a logarithmic measure of the intensity of a sound relative to the threshold of hearing: β = 10 log₁₀I/I₀, measured in decibels (dB).
The threshold of hearing I₀ = 1.0×10⁻¹² W m⁻² is the minimum intensity audible at about 1 kHz.
A difference of 10 dB corresponds to a ratio of intensities of 10; a difference of about 3 dB corresponds to a ratio of 2.
Intensity levels in dB cannot be added directly; the intensities of incoherent sources add, and the total is then converted to dB.
For a point source the intensity obeys the inverse square law, I ∝ 1/r², because the same power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr².
Intensity level uses a logarithmic scale: every tenfold increase in intensity adds 10 dB.

Beats are the periodic variations in intensity (loudness) caused by the superposition of two sound waves of slightly different frequencies.
Beats are produced because the two waves alternate between being in phase (constructive interference, loud) and in antiphase (destructive interference, soft).
The beat frequency is the number of loud (or soft) sounds heard per second and equals the magnitude of the difference between the two frequencies.
The frequency of the resultant sound is the mean of the two frequencies, and its amplitude varies at the beat frequency.
Beats can be used to compare an unknown frequency with a standard; loading or filing one source changes the beat frequency in a predictable way.
Beats: two close frequencies superpose to give an amplitude that rises and falls at f₁ − f₂.

A frequency found from a beat frequency has two possibilities, f ± f_beat. When extra information is given (loading, filing or waxing), decide which one is correct: writing both f₂ − f₁ and f₁ − f₂ is a multiple answer and scores zero. Example: f₁ = 256 Hz, f_beat = 4 Hz, and loading Q lowers the beat frequency, so f_beat = f₂ − f₁ and f₂ = 260 Hz. Give both values only if the question gives no way to decide.

Know the difference between beats and interference. Beats: superposition of two waves of slightly different frequencies; the observer does not need to move to hear loud and soft sounds. Interference: superposition of two coherent waves; the observer must move from place to place to hear loud and soft sounds.
The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency of a wave due to relative motion between the source and the observer.
When a source moves towards a stationary observer, the wavelength is shortened and the observed frequency is higher; when it moves away, the wavelength is lengthened and the frequency is lower.
When an observer moves towards a stationary source, more wavefronts are intercepted per second, so the observed frequency is higher; moving away gives a lower frequency.
Speeds are taken relative to the air (medium); the speed of sound in air is unchanged by the motion of source or observer.
The Doppler shift of waves reflected from a moving object is used in radar speed guns and in medical blood-flow measurement.
Doppler effect: wavefronts bunch up ahead of a moving source.

Geometrical optics studies light on the assumption that it travels in straight lines called rays. A collection of rays is a beam. Two laws describe how light changes direction at a surface: the law of reflection and the law of refraction.

Law of reflectionthe angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane. (Angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface.)

A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, upright, the same size (m = +1), as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (v = u), and laterally inverted. This is why “AMBULANCE” is written back to front on the front of an ambulance: it reads correctly in a driver’s mirror.

A lens is a transparent object with two refracting surfaces whose principal axes coincide. A thin lens is one whose thickness is small compared with its focal length.
Figure 23.5: converging (convex) lenses make parallel rays converge; diverging (concave) lenses make them diverge.
Principal axis: the line through the centre of the lens, perpendicular to both surfaces.
Focal point F: the point where parallel paraxial rays meet after a converging lens, or from which they appear to diverge after a diverging lens. A lens has a focal point on each side.
Focal length f: the distance between the focal point and the centre of the lens.
Ray 1: a ray parallel to the axis passes through F on the other side (converging), or appears to come from F on the same side (diverging).
Ray 2: a ray through F (or heading towards F on the far side, diverging) leaves parallel to the axis.
Ray 3: a ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on.

Sign convention used throughout (real-is-positive): distances of real objects and real images are positive; virtual images (behind the mirror) have negative v; f and R are positive for a concave mirror and negative for a convex mirror.
The centre of curvature C is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; the radius of curvature r is the radius of that sphere.
The pole P is the centre of the reflecting surface of the mirror; the aperture is the size (area) of the reflecting surface.
The principal axis is the line through the pole and the centre of curvature; it is normal to the mirror at its pole.
The principal focus of a concave mirror is the point on the principal axis through which rays parallel and close to the axis converge after reflection.
The focal length is the distance from the pole to the principal focus; f = R/2 for a spherical mirror of small aperture, where R is the radius of curvature.
Linear magnification is the ratio of the image height to the object height, m = h_i/hₒ = −v/u; m is negative for an inverted (real) image and positive for an upright (virtual) image.
A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image for u > f and a virtual, upright, magnified image for u < f; a convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.
Concave mirror: an object beyond C forms a real, inverted, diminished image between C and F.

Physical (wave) optics studies the wave nature of light: interference, diffraction and polarisation.
A wavefront is a line or surface on which all points vibrate in the same phase. Wavefronts can be plane or spherical.
A ray is a line perpendicular to the wavefronts; it shows the direction of travel of the wave.

Huygens’s principlestates that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave. The new wavefront is the surface tangent to all these wavelets.
Figure 24.1: constructing the new wavefront from the secondary wavelets, for a plane and a spherical wavefront.
Reflection · Points on the wavefront reach the mirror one after another. Their wavelets spread back from the mirror; the tangent to them is the reflected wavefront, at an equal angle (i = r).

Refraction · Wavelets in the second medium travel at a different speed, so in the same time they have a different radius. The tangent wavefront changes direction, giving Snell’s law, sin θ₁/sin θ₂ = v₁/v₂.

Diffraction · Only the part of the wavefront in the gap produces wavelets. The wavelets at the edges spread into the shadow, so the new wavefront bends round the edges. The effect is greatest when the gap is about the size of λ.
Interference · Wavelets from two (or more) coherent sources overlap. Where crests meet crests the light is bright; where crests meet troughs it is dark.
Figure 24.2: diffraction at a gap explained by Huygens’s wavelets.

Each dot in the gap is a source of wavelets. With one slit you see diffraction: narrow the slit and the waves spread more. With two slits the wavelets from both gaps interfere and give bright and dark directions.
Coherent sourcesare sources that emit waves of the same frequency (wavelength) with a constant phase difference.

Two separate lamps are not coherent: each atom emits at random, so the phase difference changes all the time. Coherent sources are made by splitting light from one source: by two slits (division of wavefront) or by partial reflection at a thin film (division of amplitude).
A clear interference pattern also needs waves of roughly the same amplitude, so that the dark fringes are really dark.
the waves meet in phase (crest on crest) · the waves meet in antiphase (crest on trough)
resultant amplitude = sum of the amplitudes: bright · resultant amplitude = difference (zero if equal): dark

Path difference: the difference between the distances travelled by the two waves from their sources to the point.
Path difference and optical path difference
A path difference of λ is a phase difference of 2π; a path difference of λ/2 is a phase difference of π. In general, Δφ = (2π/λ) × path difference.
Path difference and optical path difference
Optical path = refractive index × geometric path, nL. In a medium of index n the wavelength is λ/n, so a length L holds as many waves as a length nL in a vacuum.
Path difference and optical path difference
Optical path difference (OPD): the difference between the optical paths of the two waves. Use the OPD whenever the light goes through different media.
In 1801 Thomas Young showed interference of light with two slits. It proved that light is a wave, and it lets us measure its wavelength.
Figure 24.3: the two slits S₁ and S₂ act as coherent sources. The path difference to P is a sin θ.
Monochromatic light from one source falls on two narrow slits S₁ and S₂ a distance a apart. By diffraction, the light spreads out from each slit, and the two slits act as coherent sources in phase.

The waves overlap on a screen a distance D away. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths they interfere constructively: a bright fringe. Where it is an odd number of half wavelengths: a dark fringe.
The result is a series of equally spaced, equally bright fringes.
Figure 24.4: the two-slit pattern. All the bright fringes are about equally bright and equally spaced.

The colours of soap bubbles and oil films come from interference between light reflected from the top and the bottom surfaces of a thin transparent film (division of amplitude).

The extra path: ray 2 travels an extra distance 2t inside the film, an optical path difference of 2nt.

Phase change on reflection: light reflected at a boundary with a medium of higher refractive index undergoes a phase change of π (equivalent to an extra λ/2). Reflection at a boundary with a lower refractive index gives no phase change.

Diffractionis the spreading of waves when they pass through an aperture or round the edge of an obstacle. It is the result of interference between wavelets from different points on the same wavefront.
Figure 24.6: the single-slit pattern. The central maximum is twice as wide as the others and much brighter.
Central maximum: straight ahead (θ = 0), all the wavelets from the slit travel the same distance and arrive in phase, so they interfere constructively.

First minimum: divide the slit into two halves. If the bottom edge is λ further from the screen than the top edge, each wavelet in the top half is λ/2 ahead of the matching wavelet in the bottom half. They cancel in pairs, so no light arrives.
Second minimum: divide the slit into four parts; neighbouring parts cancel. In general minima occur at a sin θ = mλ, m = ±1, ±2, …
Between the minima there are weaker secondary maxima, at about a sin θ ≈ (m + ½)λ.
Figure 24.7: the first minimum of a single slit of width a.

Because of diffraction, the image of a point source formed through an aperture is not a point but a small spread-out pattern. Two close sources may overlap so much that they cannot be seen as separate.
Rayleigh’s criterion: two sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one diffraction pattern falls on the first minimum of the other.
The smaller the angle θ between two sources that can still be resolved, the greater the resolving power.
Change the slit width and the wavelength and watch the central maximum. Then switch on a second source and move the two sources closer until they are only just resolved.
A diffraction grating has a very large number of equally spaced, parallel, narrow slits. A transmission grating can be made by ruling many fine lines on glass; a CD acts as a reflection grating.
Grating spacing d = distance between the centres of adjacent slits = 1/N, where N = number of lines per unit length. e.g. 5000 lines per cm: d = 1/5000 cm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Figure 24.9: monochromatic light gives sharp bright lines (orders) at definite angles.

Monochromatic light falls normally on the grating. By Huygens’s principle each slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
Formation of the pattern and the grating equation

In most directions the wavelets from the many slits cancel. Only in directions where the path difference between wavelets from adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths do they all interfere constructively.

This gives very sharp, bright lines (principal maxima) with almost complete darkness between them, much sharper than with two slits.

Figure 24.10: the path difference between adjacent slits.
The zero order (θ = 0) is white, because every wavelength has θ = 0 there.
In every other order, each wavelength is diffracted at a different angle (sin θ = mλ/d), so the colours separate into a spectrum: violet nearest the centre, red furthest out.
Higher orders are more spread out and may overlap (e.g. the red of the 2nd order with the violet of the 3rd).
Change the number of lines per mm and the wavelength, or choose white light. See the angles of each order and the highest order possible.
Every point on the wavefront at each slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
The new wavefront is the line touching the wavelets; it bends round the edges of each slit (diffraction).
The diffracted waves from all the slits overlap and interfere.

Where the path difference between adjacent slits is mλ, the waves are in phase and give a bright fringe. (Draw at least three slits with circular wavelets, and new wavefronts in two different directions.)
Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave: its electric field E vibrates perpendicular to the direction of travel.
In unpolarised light (sunlight, a lamp) the electric field vibrates in all directions perpendicular to the direction of travel.
In plane-polarised light the electric field vibrates in one plane only.
Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation is evidence that light is a transverse wave; sound (longitudinal) cannot be polarised.

A polariser (e.g. Polaroid sheet) has long-chain molecules aligned in one direction, giving it a transmission axis. Only the component of E parallel to the axis passes; the perpendicular component is absorbed.
Unpolarised light through one polariser becomes plane-polarised, and its intensity is halved: I = I₀/2.
Figure 24.11: a polariser and an analyser.

Malus’s lawstates that when plane-polarised light of intensity I₀ passes through an analyser whose transmission axis is at angle θ to the plane of polarisation, the transmitted intensity is I = I₀ cos² θ.
Turn the analyser and watch the transmitted intensity follow I = I₀ cos²θ. Add a third polariser between two crossed ones: light gets through again.
Unpolarised light reflected from glass or water is partially polarised.

At one angle of incidence, the Brewster angle θ_B, the reflected light is completely plane-polarised (vibrating parallel to the surface). At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
Figure 24.12: at the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are at 90°.
Polaroid sunglasses cut glare: light reflected from water and roads is mostly horizontally polarised, and the lenses block it.
LCD screens use two polarisers with liquid crystal between them to control each pixel.
Photography filters reduce reflections and darken blue sky; stress analysis shows strain patterns in transparent models; 3-D cinema glasses send a different image to each eye.
Total internal reflection: when light in a denser medium hits the boundary with a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle c (sin c = n₂/n₁), all the light is reflected.
An optical fibre has a glass core of higher refractive index n₁ surrounded by a cladding of lower index n₂.

Light entering within the acceptance angle strikes the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected again and again. It is guided along the core with very little loss, even round gentle bends.
The cladding protects the core surface and stops light leaking into a neighbouring fibre.
Figure 24.13: light guided along an optical fibre by repeated total internal reflection.
Telecommunications · telephone, television and internet signals travel as light pulses: high bandwidth, low loss, no electrical interference
Medicine · endoscopes let doctors see inside the body; fibres also carry laser light for surgery
Sensing · changes in the light show changes in temperature, pressure or strain
Others · decorative lighting, inspection cameras in hard-to-reach places

Young’s double slit with a thin film over one slit
Without the film, S₁O = S₂O, so O is the central bright fringe (path difference 0). The 5th bright fringe P₅ is where S₂P − S₁P = 5λ.
In the film, light slows to c/n but its frequency does not change, so its wavelength shrinks to λ/n.
More waves fit into the thickness t: t/λ waves in air, but nt/λ waves in the film. Optical path = n × thickness.
The film replaces a layer of air of the same thickness. Extra optical path = nt − t = (n − 1)t, not nt. Check: n = 1 gives no change.
The central fringe still needs zero total path difference, so it moves towards the covered slit, to where S₂P − S₁P = (n − 1)t. The fringe separation does not change.
It lands on the old 5th bright fringe: (n − 1)t = 5λ, so t = 5(590 × 10⁻⁹) / (1.50 − 1) = 5.90 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Young’s double slit: measure every fringe from the central bright fringe O
Count from the central bright fringe O. O is the 0th bright fringe, not the 1st.
The nth bright fringe is nΔy from O.
The nth dark fringe is (n − ½)Δy from O. The 1st dark fringe is only ½Δy from O.
Find the distance of each fringe from O first. Same side of O: subtract. Opposite sides: add.

Wavefront is a line or surface joining all points of a wave that are in phase (same displacement and same direction of motion).

Huygens's principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront after a short time t is the envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave into the geometrical shadow when it passes the edge of an obstacle or through a gap; the points at the edge act as sources of secondary wavelets that spread into the shadow region.

Reflection and refraction: construction with secondary wavelets gives the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and Snell's law; on refraction the frequency is unchanged while the speed and wavelength change.
Huygens's principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets; the new wavefront is their envelope.
Wave speed · v = fλ · v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m)

Refractive index · n = c/v = λ₀/λ · n = refractive index of the medium (no unit); c = speed in vacuum (m s⁻¹); v = speed in the medium (m s⁻¹); λ₀ = wavelength in vacuum (air) (m); λ = wavelength in the medium (m)
Snell's law · n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ · n₁, n₂ = refractive indices of the two media; θ₁, θ₂ = angles measured from the normal
Wavelet radius · r = vt · Distance moved by a wavefront in time t, which is the radius of each secondary wavelet; v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); t = time (s)

State that the secondary wavelets have the same speed and frequency as the original wave.
For diffraction, state that the edge points act as sources and the wavelets spread into the region behind the obstacle.

Principle of superposition: when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of the individual waves at that point.
Interference is the superposition of two or more coherent waves, producing a pattern of reinforcement (maxima) and cancellation (minima).
Coherent sources are sources that emit waves of the same frequency (wavelength) with a constant phase difference.

Optical path between two points in a medium is the distance in vacuum that contains the same number of wavelengths as the medium between the two points, for light of the same frequency; optical path = nd, where n is the refractive index and d the actual distance.
Constructive interference occurs when the waves meet in phase (path difference = nλ, n = 0, 1, 2, …); destructive interference occurs when they meet in antiphase (path difference = (n + ½)λ).
Two separate light bulbs do not give a stable interference pattern because the phase relationship of their light changes randomly and rapidly, so they are not coherent.

On reflection from a medium of higher refractive index (denser medium) the wave undergoes a phase change of π (equivalent to a path change of λ/2); there is no phase change on reflection at a less dense medium.
Interference from two coherent sources: bright where path difference = mλ.
Constructive interference · Δ = nλ · Δ = path difference (m); λ = wavelength (m); n = 0, 1, 2, …
Destructive interference · Δ = (n + ½)λ · Δ = path difference (m); λ = wavelength (m); n = 0, 1, 2, …
Phase difference · φ = 2π/λ × Δ · φ = phase difference (rad); Δ = path difference (m); λ = wavelength (m)
Intensity and amplitude · I ∝ A² · I = intensity (W m⁻²); A = amplitude
Maximum and minimum intensity · Iₘₐₓ = (√I₁ + √I₂)²; I_min = (√I₁ − √I₂)² · Two coherent waves of intensities I₁ and I₂ (W m⁻²)
Maximum and minimum amplitude · Aₘₐₓ = A₁ + A₂; A_min = |A₁ − A₂| · Amplitudes add; A₁, A₂ = amplitudes of the two waves
For path difference questions: divide Δ by λ. A whole number gives a bright (maximum); a half-integer gives a dark (minimum). State the conclusion with the value of Δ/λ.
For 'explain why no pattern' state: the sources are not coherent, i.e. the phase difference is not constant.
For an intensity ratio: add and subtract the square roots of the intensities (amplitudes), then square.
Mention any phase change of π on reflection before deciding between maximum and minimum.

Young's double-slit experiment: light from a single narrow slit (or a laser) illuminates two narrow slits S₁ and S₂ which act as coherent sources; the overlapping diffracted waves produce alternate bright and dark fringes on a screen.
The bright fringe is formed where the path difference S₂P − S₁P = nλ; the dark fringe where S₂P − S₁P = (n + ½)λ.
Fringes are equally spaced and of nearly equal brightness near the centre; the central fringe (n = 0) is bright because the path difference is zero.
With white light, the central fringe is white and the other fringes are coloured (violet nearest the centre, red furthest) since fringe spacing ∝ λ.
Young's double slits: fringe separation x = λD/a.
Fringe spacing · x = λD/a · x = fringe spacing (m); λ = wavelength (m); D = slit-to-screen distance (m); a = slit separation (m); valid for D ≫ a
Path difference at a point · Δ = ay/D · Δ = path difference (m); y = distance from the central fringe (m)
Bright fringe position · yₙ = nλD/a · yₙ = position of the nth bright fringe (m); n = 0, 1, 2, …
Dark fringe position · yₙ = ((n + ½)λD)/(a) · yₙ = position of the nth dark fringe (m)
Angular position of bright fringe · a sin θ = nλ · θ = angular position of the nth bright fringe; a = slit separation (m); λ = wavelength (m)
Wavelength and spacing in a medium · λ′ = λ/n; x′ = x/n · In a medium of refractive index n; λ′ = wavelength in the medium (m); x′ = fringe spacing in the medium (m)
Start from x = λD/a, rearrange for the unknown, convert mm and nm to m, substitute with units, give 3 s.f.
For 'distance between the mth and the nth fringes' use (n − m)x, not n x or m x separately.
For effects of changing a quantity, state the proportionality: x ∝ λ, x ∝ D, x ∝ 1/a, then the new value.
State assumptions: slits narrow, a ≪ D so that sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ.

Thin-film interference is the interference between the light reflected from the top surface and the light reflected from the bottom surface of the film; the two beams are coherent because they originate from the same incident wave.
A phase change of π occurs on reflection when the light is reflected from a medium of higher refractive index; there is no phase change on reflection from a medium of lower refractive index.
Colours of a thin film in white light: the film thickness varies, so different wavelengths satisfy the condition for constructive interference at different places, giving coloured bands.

Air wedge: the air layer between two glass plates in contact at one edge; the fringes are straight, parallel and equally spaced, and the fringe at the line of contact is dark because of the π phase change at one reflection only.
Non-reflective coating: a thin film of refractive index between those of air and glass; the reflected beams from the two surfaces interfere destructively so that reflection is reduced.
Thin film: light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces interferes; count the π phase changes.
Thin film, one phase change: constructive · 2nt = (m + ½)λ · Film of index n in air, one phase change at the top surface; t = film thickness (m); λ = wavelength in air (m); m = 0, 1, 2, …
Thin film, one phase change: destructive · 2nt = mλ · Film of index n in air, one phase change at the top surface; m = 0, 1, 2, …
Thin film, no relative phase change: constructive · 2nt = mλ · Both reflections with a π change, or neither (e.g. coating on glass with n_air < n_film < n_glass)
Thin film, no relative phase change: destructive · 2nt = (m + ½)λ · Both reflections with a π change, or neither (e.g. coating on glass with n_air < n_film < n_glass)
Minimum coating thickness · t = λ/4n · Minimum coating thickness for destructive reflection of wavelength λ (m); n = refractive index of the coating
Air wedge dark fringes · 2t = mλ · Air wedge at normal incidence; dark fringes; t = air gap thickness (m); m = 0, 1, 2, …
Air wedge fringe spacing · x = λ/2θ · Air wedge at normal incidence; x = fringe spacing (m); θ = wedge angle (rad)
First decide the number of π phase changes at the two surfaces (list n₁, n₂, n₃ in order), then write the correct condition.
State that the optical path difference is 2nt (the beam travels t down and t up inside the film) and that λ in the formula is the wavelength in air (the n is already included).
Rearrange for t or λ, substitute, give the answer with unit, and name the order m used.
For 'explain the colours', mention variation in thickness and the condition for each wavelength.

Do not assume the minimum thickness is always λ/4n. First decide whether the reflected light interferes constructively or destructively, and whether there is a coating. Film in air (one phase change): destructive t_min = λ/2n, constructive t_min = λ/4n. Coating on glass (two phase changes): destructive t_min = λ/4n, constructive t_min = λ/2n.

Example: red and blue light fall on a soap film (n = 1.33) in air and the reflected light appears red. "Appears red" means the blue is cancelled, so blue interferes destructively: t_min = λ_blue/2n = 465 (nm)/(2 × 1.33) = 175 nm.
Diffraction is the spreading of waves when they pass through a gap or round an obstacle; it is most marked when the width of the gap is comparable with the wavelength.
A single-slit diffraction pattern has a wide, bright central maximum with weaker secondary maxima on both sides; the intensity of the secondary maxima falls rapidly.
The pattern arises from interference between the secondary wavelets from different points across the width of the slit.
The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum; the minima occur where the path difference between the two edges of the slit is a whole number of wavelengths.
Single-slit pattern: a wide, bright central maximum (twice the width of the others); first minima at sin θ = λ/a.
Single-slit minima · a sin θ = mλ · m = 1, 2, 3, … for the minima; a = slit width (m); θ = angle from the central axis (rad or °); λ = wavelength (m)
Angular width of central maximum · 2θ₁; sin θ₁ = λ/a · 2θ₁ = angular width of the central maximum (rad); θ₁ = angle of the first minimum; a = slit width (m); λ = wavelength (m)
Width of central maximum on screen · w = 2λD/a · small angles; w = width of the central maximum (m); D = distance from slit to screen (m); λ = wavelength (m); a = slit width (m)
Small-angle approximation · θ ≈ λ/a · for small angles; θ = angle of the first minimum (rad); λ = wavelength (m); a = slit width (m)
Write the condition for minima first (a sin θ = mλ), then substitute with values converted to metres.
For the width of the central maximum, double the distance from the centre to the first minimum: w = 2λD/a. State clearly 'width' versus 'half-width'.
For 'what happens when a decreases', state: sin θ increases so the central maximum becomes wider (and less intense).
A sketch of intensity against angle needs a labelled axis, a tall central peak that is twice the width of the others and small secondary peaks.

Diffraction grating is an optical device with a large number of equally spaced parallel slits (lines) of very narrow width; the diffracted beams interfere to produce sharp, bright maxima at definite angles.
Grating spacing d is the distance between the centres of adjacent slits; d = 1/N, where N is the number of lines per unit length.
The maxima occur where the path difference between light from adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths.
With white light, the zero-order maximum is white and each higher order is a spectrum with violet nearest and red furthest from the centre; the higher orders may overlap.
Increasing the number of lines illuminated makes the maxima sharper and brighter; the angular positions of the maxima depend on d and λ only.
Diffraction grating: maxima at d sin θ = mλ; more lines give sharper, brighter maxima.
Grating equation · d sin θ = mλ · m = 0, 1, 2, … (order); d = grating spacing (m); θ = angle of the mth order from the normal (rad or °); λ = wavelength (m)
Grating spacing · d = 1/N · N = number of lines per metre (m⁻¹); d = grating spacing (m); for example 500 lines mm⁻¹ = 5.00 × 10⁵ lines m⁻¹, d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m
Highest order · mₘₐₓ < d/λ · mₘₐₓ = largest integer less than d/λ (because sin θ < 1); d = grating spacing (m); λ = wavelength (m)
Total number of maxima · 2mₘₐₓ + 1 · total number of maxima observed; mₘₐₓ = highest order
Grating angle from screen · tan θ = y/D · y = distance on the screen from the central maximum (m); D = distance from grating to screen (m); then find sin θ from θ
Calculate d from the number of lines per mm or cm FIRST, in metres, then apply d sin θ = mλ.
For the maximum order, evaluate d/λ and take the whole number part; state that sin θ cannot exceed 1.
When the distance y on the screen is given, find θ = tan⁻¹y/D, then use sin θ in the grating equation (do not use y/D directly for sin θ unless the angle is small).
State the answer to 3 s.f. with the order m used.
Total number of maxima = 2mₘₐₓ + 1 (both sides plus the central maximum). For d/λ = 3.99, mₘₐₓ = 3, so 7 maxima are seen.
Plane-polarised (linearly polarised) light is light in which the electric field vibrations are in one plane only, perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

Unpolarised light is light whose electric field vibrations occur in all planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation; it can be resolved into two mutually perpendicular components of equal intensity, both perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Plane of polarisation is the plane containing the electric field vibrations of the wave and the direction of propagation.
Only transverse waves can be polarised; the polarisation of light shows that light is a transverse wave, whereas sound (a longitudinal wave) cannot be polarised.
Polariser produces plane-polarised light from unpolarised light; analyser is a second polariser used to detect the plane of polarisation.

Malus's law: the intensity of plane-polarised light transmitted through an analyser is proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between the plane of polarisation of the light and the transmission axis of the analyser.

Brewster's law: when light is incident at the polarising angle θ_B, the reflected light is completely plane-polarised (vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence) and the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other.
Unpolarised light passing through an ideal polariser is reduced to half of the incident intensity.
Malus's law: a polariser transmits I₀ cos²θ of plane-polarised light.

Malus's law · I = I₀ cos² θ · I₀ = intensity of plane-polarised light incident on the analyser (W m⁻²); I = transmitted intensity (W m⁻²); θ = angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis

Unpolarised light through a polariser · I₁ = (I_unpolarised)/(2) · I₁ = intensity after the first polariser (W m⁻²); I_unpolarised = incident intensity (W m⁻²); then apply Malus's law for each further polariser
Brewster's law · tan θ_B = n₂/n₁; tan θ_B = n · θ_B = Brewster (polarising) angle; n₁, n₂ = refractive indices of the first and second media; tan θ_B = n for light incident from air
Reflected and refracted rays at Brewster angle · θ_B + θ_r = 90° · θ_B = Brewster angle; θ_r = angle of refraction
For unpolarised light: halve the intensity at the first polariser, then apply I = I₀ cos² θ at each later polariser, using the angle between successive axes.
For three polarisers, multiply the cos² factors of successive pairs of axes (do not use the angle to the first axis for the third).
For Brewster: state tan θ_B = n, substitute, and give θ_B in degrees; mention that the reflected ray is completely polarised.
Name the type of wave: only transverse waves can be polarised.

Know the four methods of polarisation: selective absorption (Polaroid), reflection (and transmission) at a transparent medium, double refraction (calcite, quartz) and scattering (by the Earth’s atmosphere). Malus’s law and Brewster’s angle are asked most often.
The "transmission axis" and the "polarising axis" of a polariser mean the same thing.

In a Brewster diagram, show unpolarised light with equal numbers of arrows and dots; the reflected ray has dots only (vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence), and the reflected and refracted rays are at 90°.
Optical fibre is a thin strand of glass or plastic consisting of a core surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index; light is guided along the core by total internal reflection.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
Critical angle θ_c is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is 90°.
Conditions for guiding: n_core > n_cladding and the angle of incidence at the core–cladding boundary greater than θ_c.
Attenuation is the loss of power as the signal travels along the fibre, caused by absorption and scattering in the glass.
Modal dispersion is the spreading (broadening) of a pulse because rays following different paths take different times; it is reduced in a very narrow core (single-mode) fibre or a graded-index fibre.
Optical fibre: light stays in the core by total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.
Critical angle · sin θ_c = n₂/n₁ · θ_c = critical angle; n₁ = refractive index of the core; n₂ = refractive index of the cladding
Numerical aperture · NA = sin θₐ = √n₁² − n₂² · θₐ = maximum acceptance angle (from air); NA = numerical aperture (no unit); n₁ = refractive index of the core; n₂ = refractive index of the cladding
Attenuation · Attenuation = 10/L log₁₀(P_in)/(P_out) · in dB per unit length; L = length of the fibre; P_in = input power (W); P_out = output power (W)

Pulse transit time along axis · t = L/v = nL/c · t = time for a pulse along the axis (s); L = length of the fibre (m); v = c/n = speed of light in the core (m s⁻¹); n = refractive index of the core; c = speed of light in vacuum (m s⁻¹)
Identify n₁ (core, larger) and n₂ (cladding, smaller) before using sin θ_c = n₂/n₁; the ratio must be less than 1.
For NA: substitute the two indices, give 3 s.f.; a numerical aperture is dimensionless.
For an explanation of guiding, state both conditions: core index greater than cladding index AND angle of incidence at the boundary greater than the critical angle.
For a time along the fibre, use v = c/n, not v = c.
A black body is an ideal object that absorbs all the electromagnetic radiation falling on it, and is also the best possible emitter.
The spectrum of a hot body shows that (a) the total energy emitted (area under the curve) increases with temperature, and (b) the peak wavelength becomes shorter as the temperature increases.
Classical physics assumed energy is continuous and predicted that the intensity rises without limit at short wavelengths. This disagreed with experiment.
Figure 25.1: black-body spectra and the failed classical prediction.

Planck’s quantum theoryelectromagnetic radiation is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets of energy called quanta. The energy of one quantum is proportional to the frequency of the radiation: E = hf.
An oscillator can only have energies 0, hf, 2hf, 3hf, …: the energy is quantised.
Einstein (1905) proposed that light itself travels as quanta called photons. A photon has no mass, travels at c in a vacuum and carries energy hf.
Electronvolt: the kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
energy depends on the intensity (∝ amplitude²) · energy of one photon depends on frequency: E = hf
energy is continuous and spread through the wave · energy comes in discrete packets
Photoelectric effectis the emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency falls on it. The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.
Figure 25.2: apparatus for the photoelectric effect.
Monochromatic light falls on the emitter (cathode) in an evacuated tube. Photoelectrons travel to the collector (anode) and a photocurrent I flows.
As the positive voltage increases, more photoelectrons reach the collector, until all of them do: the current reaches a maximum, the saturation current.
Even at V = 0 a small current flows, because some photoelectrons have enough kinetic energy to reach the collector.
If the supply is reversed, the collector repels the electrons. The current falls to zero at the stopping potential Vₛ.
Stopping potential, Vₛis the minimum reverse potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons from reaching the collector.
Figure 25.3: current against voltage for two intensities of the same frequency.
No electrons are emitted if the frequency is below a threshold frequency f₀, however intense the light.
Above f₀, emission is instantaneous, even for very weak light.
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (and so Vₛ) increases with frequency, but does not depend on intensity.
The photocurrent (number of electrons per second) is proportional to the intensity.
any frequency can eject electrons if the light is intense enough · no emission below the threshold frequency, however intense the light
the maximum kinetic energy increases with intensity · the maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency
with weak light there should be a delay while energy builds up · emission is instantaneous
An electron absorbs the energy of one photon, all at once.
Some energy, at least the work function W, is needed to free the electron from the metal. The rest becomes kinetic energy.

Work function W: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal. Threshold frequency f₀: the minimum frequency that can eject an electron, W = hf₀. Threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/f₀ is the maximum wavelength.
More intense light means more photons per second, so more electrons per second (more current), but each photon still has the same energy.
Figure 25.4: K_max against f is a straight line of gradient h; V_s against f has gradient h/e for every metal, with different threshold frequencies.

Choose a metal and change the wavelength, intensity and voltage. Below the threshold frequency no electrons come out, however bright the light. Find the stopping potential by making the voltage negative until the current is zero.
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell
The photovoltaic effect is the production of an e.m.f. across a p–n junction of a semiconductor when it absorbs light.
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell
A photon with energy at least equal to the band gap is absorbed near the junction and creates an electron–hole pair.
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell

The electric field at the junction separates the electrons (to the n side) and holes (to the p side) before they recombine, so an e.m.f. appears across the cell and drives a current in an external circuit.
Photovoltaic effect in a solar cell

Unlike the photoelectric effect, no electron leaves the material: the charge carriers are collected inside the cell. Solar cells convert light energy directly into electrical energy with no moving parts; many cells form a solar panel.
Light behaves as a wave in interference and diffraction, and as a particle (photons) in the photoelectric effect. De Broglie suggested that particles might also behave as waves.
de Broglie’s hypothesisa moving particle has a wave associated with it, whose wavelength is λ = h/p, where p = mv is the momentum of the particle.
Figure 25.5: electrons passing through a thin graphite film form diffraction rings.
Electrons are accelerated through a few kilovolts and pass through a thin graphite film.
The rows of carbon atoms act like a diffraction grating, because their spacing is similar to the electron wavelength.
Bright rings appear on the fluorescent screen: a diffraction pattern. Diffraction is a wave property, so this is evidence that electrons behave as waves.

When the accelerating voltage increases, the rings become smaller: the electrons are faster, so λ = h/mv is shorter, as de Broglie predicted. (Davisson and Germer first showed electron diffraction in 1927.)
Change the accelerating voltage. A higher voltage gives faster electrons, a shorter de Broglie wavelength and smaller diffraction rings.
The resolving power of a microscope is limited by diffraction: the minimum resolvable detail is about the wavelength used.
Electrons accelerated through tens of kilovolts have wavelengths of about 10⁻¹¹ m, thousands of times shorter than visible light (about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m).
So an electron microscope has a much higher resolving power than an optical microscope and can show much finer detail.

Figure 25.6: the Coulomb force provides the centripetal force on the orbiting electron.
Ground state (n = 1): the lowest energy level. Excited states: n = 2, 3, 4, …
Excitation energy: the energy needed to move an electron from the ground state to a higher level, e.g. E₂ − E₁ = 10.2 eV.
Ionisation energy: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the ground state completely (to n = ∞): 13.6 eV for hydrogen.
Figure 25.7: energy levels of hydrogen and three series of emission lines.

Emission: atoms of a low-pressure gas are excited (by heating or by an electric discharge). When an electron falls from a higher level to a lower level, it emits a photon of energy hf = E_i − E_f. Only certain energy differences exist, so only certain wavelengths are emitted: bright lines on a dark background.

Absorption: white light passes through a cool gas. Photons whose energy exactly equals an energy difference are absorbed, raising electrons to higher levels: dark lines on a continuous spectrum, at the same wavelengths as the emission lines.
Lyman series: transitions ending at n = 1 (ultraviolet). Balmer series: ending at n = 2 (visible). Paschen: ending at n = 3 (infrared). Brackett (n = 4) and Pfund (n = 5): infrared.
Pick the starting and final levels. A fall emits a photon; a jump up absorbs one. The wavelength and series are shown, and visible lines appear in the spectrum.

X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about 10⁻¹² m to 10⁻⁸ m), discovered by Röntgen in 1895. They travel in straight lines, penetrate matter, are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, ionise gases, affect photographic film, cause fluorescence and can be diffracted.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
A heated filament (cathode) emits electrons by thermionic emission.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
A high voltage (tens of kV) accelerates them across an evacuated tube, so they do not collide with gas molecules.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
They strike a target of a heavy metal with a high melting point (tungsten or molybdenum). Less than 1% of their kinetic energy becomes X-rays; the rest becomes heat, so the target is cooled.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
The tube current (filament current) controls the number of electrons, so the intensity of the X-rays. The accelerating voltage controls the electron energy, so the penetrating power (hardness).
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Figure 25.9: an X-ray spectrum: a continuous spectrum with a sharp cut-off at λ_min, and characteristic lines.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Electrons are decelerated by the nuclei of the target atoms; the kinetic energy lost is emitted as an X-ray photon.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
An electron can lose any amount of energy in a collision, so all wavelengths above a minimum are produced.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
The shortest wavelength comes from an electron that loses all its kinetic energy in one collision.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
A fast electron knocks out an electron from an inner shell (e.g. K shell) of a target atom, leaving a vacancy.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
An electron from a higher shell falls into the vacancy and emits an X-ray photon of energy equal to the difference of the two energy levels.
Production of X-rays in an X-ray tube
The energies are fixed for each element, so the lines are characteristic of the target metal. Kα: L → K; Kβ: M → K; Lα: M → L, …
tube current increased · intensity increases; λ_min unchanged · more intense; same wavelengths
accelerating voltage increased · intensity increases; λ_min decreases · same wavelengths (may appear once eV is large enough)
target of higher atomic number · λ_min unchanged (more intense) · lines move to shorter wavelengths

Change the accelerating voltage, the tube current and the target. Watch the cut-off wavelength λmin = hc/eV move, and see the characteristic lines appear once the electrons have enough energy to knock out K-shell electrons.
The regularly spaced atoms of a crystal act like a diffraction grating for X-rays, because the spacing of the atomic planes (about 10⁻¹⁰ m) is similar to the X-ray wavelength.
X-rays are partly reflected by each plane of atoms. Waves reflected from adjacent planes interfere constructively when their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
Figure 25.10: reflection from two adjacent atomic planes a distance d apart. θ is the glancing angle, measured from the plane.
Change the glancing angle, the plane spacing and the wavelength. The detector reading is high only when 2d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths.
Medicine · radiography of bones and organs; CT scans; radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells
Industry · non-destructive testing of welds, castings and pipes; X-ray crystallography of materials
Security · baggage and cargo scanning at airports
Research · crystal structures of DNA and proteins; X-ray astronomy

The tube current (a few mA) is set by heating the filament: a hotter filament emits more electrons per second, so more X-ray photons are produced and the picture is brighter. It does not change λ_min.
The tube voltage (about 50–120 kV) sets the energy of each electron, eV, and so the most energetic photons. Higher voltage gives more penetrating ("harder") X-rays.

Bone contains calcium, which has a higher atomic number than soft tissue, so it absorbs X-rays much more strongly. Where X-rays reach the detector it turns dark; behind bone it stays light. That is why bones look white on an X-ray image.
About 99% of the electrons' energy becomes heat in the target, so the anode is made of tungsten and is often a spinning disc, so the heat is spread around its rim.

Turn on the tube and watch an X-ray image build up. The filament current controls how many electrons (and photons) there are each second; the voltage controls the energy of each one. At low voltage even the soft tissue blocks most X-rays; at high voltage the bones become less clear.
Nanoscienceis the study of structures and materials on the scale of about 1 nm to 100 nm (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, a few atoms across). Nanotechnology is the design and making of devices at this scale.

At the nanoscale, materials can behave very differently from the bulk: a large fraction of the atoms are at the surface, and quantum effects become important. Colour, strength, conductivity and chemical reactivity can all change with size.
Examples: carbon nanotubes and graphene (very strong, excellent conductors), quantum dots (nanocrystals whose colour depends on their size), nanoparticles of titanium dioxide and silver.
Microprocessors · transistors only a few nanometres wide: billions on one chip, faster and using less power
Memory and data storage · nanoscale memory cells and magnetic layers store far more data in a smaller space (flash memory, hard disks)
Displays · quantum-dot (QLED) screens give bright, pure colours; organic and flexible displays
Sensors · nanoscale sensors detect tiny amounts of gases, chemicals or biological molecules
Solar cells and batteries · nanostructured materials absorb more light and store more charge
Future electronics · graphene and carbon-nanotube transistors; single-electron devices
Other applications: stain-resistant fabrics, scratch-resistant paint, self-cleaning glass, drug delivery and early detection of disease.
Concerns: nanoparticles may be breathed in or absorbed through the skin, and their effects on health and the environment are not yet fully understood.
