Animated fixes for the mistakes students make most often in this chapter.
Electrons leave the heated filament by thermionic emission.
A high p.d. V accelerates them across the vacuum, so each gains kinetic energy eV.
Electrons decelerate in the target and emit a continuous spectrum (bremsstrahlung).
The shortest wavelength is λ_min, when all of eV becomes one photon.
Characteristic lines: an electron knocks out a K-shell electron, an outer electron drops into the gap and emits a photon of fixed energy.
Increase V: λ_min decreases and intensity increases. The lines do not move.
Change the target metal: the lines move. λ_min stays the same.
About 99% of the energy becomes heat, so the anode must be cooled.
Stopping potential is a potential difference. Its unit is V, never eV.
The electronvolt (eV) is a unit of energy: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
At the stopping potential the fastest photoelectrons just fail to reach the collector, so the photocurrent is zero.
eVₛ = Kₘₐₓ, so Kₘₐₓ = 1.96 eV gives Vₛ = 1.96 V.
Photon is a quantum (packet) of electromagnetic radiation of energy E = hf; it is a neutral particle with zero rest mass that travels at the speed of light.
Photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency falls on it.
Compton effect is the scattering of X-ray photons by electrons in atoms; the scattered photon has a longer wavelength (lower energy) than the incident photon, showing that a photon carries momentum.
Work function φ is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal; threshold frequency f₀ is the minimum frequency for emission, f₀ = φ/h.
Stopping potential Vₛ is the minimum reverse potential difference that reduces the photocurrent to zero; eVₛ = Kₘₐₓ.
Einstein's photoelectric equation: hf = φ + Kₘₐₓ, an electron absorbs one photon whose energy is shared between the work function and the kinetic energy.
Observations that wave theory cannot explain: a threshold frequency exists; Kₘₐₓ is independent of intensity and depends on frequency; emission is instantaneous.
Photoelectric effect: KEmax rises linearly with frequency above the threshold f₀; the gradient is h.
Photon energy · E = hf = hc/λ · E = photon energy (J); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹

Photoelectric equation · hf = φ + ½mv²_max; φ = hf₀ · f = frequency of incident radiation (Hz); φ = work function (J); f₀ = threshold frequency (Hz); m = electron mass (kg); vₘₐₓ = maximum speed of photoelectrons (m s⁻¹)
Stopping potential · eVₛ = ½mv²_max = hf − φ · Vₛ = stopping potential (V); e = electron charge (C); m = electron mass (kg); vₘₐₓ = maximum speed of photoelectrons (m s⁻¹); φ = work function (J)
Photon momentum · p = h/λ · p = photon momentum (kg m s⁻¹); h = Planck constant (J s); λ = wavelength (m)
Electronvolt · 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; E (eV) ≈ (1240)/(λ) (nm) · E (eV) = photon energy in electronvolts; λ (nm) = wavelength in nanometres
Graph of Kₘₐₓ against f: straight line, gradient = h, intercept on the f-axis = f₀, intercept on the energy axis = −φ.
Write E = hf or hc/λ, convert nm to m and eV to J (or J to eV) consistently, then substitute with units.
For photoelectric questions write hf = φ + Kₘₐₓ, then Kₘₐₓ = hf − φ; convert both energies to the same unit before subtracting.
For explanations: state that intensity ∝ number of photons per second ∝ number of photoelectrons per second, and Kₘₐₓ depends on frequency only.
Say 'below the threshold frequency no emission occurs, no matter how intense the light'.

Be ready for an essay on the photoelectric effect: describe the experiment, explain why the wave theory fails to explain the results, and apply Einstein’s equation (with threshold frequency and work function).
Wave-particle duality: radiation and matter exhibit both wave properties (diffraction, interference) and particle properties (photoelectric effect, photon momentum) depending on the experiment.
de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p.
Wave nature of electrons is shown by electron diffraction through a thin crystal or graphite film (Davisson–Germer experiment): a ring (diffraction) pattern is formed.
Particle nature of light is shown by the photoelectric effect; wave nature of light by diffraction and interference.
The wave behaviour of macroscopic objects is not observed because the de Broglie wavelength is far too small compared with any obstacle or gap.
Electron diffraction rings show that electrons behave as waves with λ = h/p.
de Broglie wavelength · λ = h/p = h/mv · λ = de Broglie wavelength (m); h = Planck constant (J s); p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m s⁻¹)
Wavelength from kinetic energy · p = √2mK; λ = (h)/(√2mK) · K = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); λ = wavelength (m)

Electron accelerated through a potential difference · eV = ½mv²; λ = (h)/(√2meV) · V = accelerating potential difference (V); e = electron charge (C); m = electron mass (kg); v = speed (m s⁻¹); λ = wavelength (m)
Constants: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
Write λ = h/mv (or (h)/(√2meV)), substitute with SI units and give the answer in metres to 3 s.f. (2 s.f. if the data are 2 s.f.).
For evidence of both natures name the experiment AND the property shown: diffraction/interference → wave; photoelectric effect → particle.
For an electron accelerated through V, first find the speed or momentum from eV = ½mv², then λ = h/p.
State: a larger momentum gives a shorter wavelength (λ ∝ 1/p).

Line spectrum consists of discrete bright lines (emission) or dark lines (absorption) of definite wavelengths, characteristic of the element; it shows that electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels.

Bohr's postulates: electrons move in certain stable orbits without radiating energy (stationary states); the angular momentum of an orbiting electron is quantised, mvr = nh/2π; radiation is emitted or absorbed only when an electron makes a transition between two levels, hf = E_i − E_f.
Energy level is the energy of an electron in an allowed orbit in the atom.
Ground state is the state in which the electron in the atom has the lowest energy (n = 1); an excited state is any state with energy higher than the ground state.
Excitation energy is the energy needed to raise an electron from the ground state to an excited state.
Ionisation energy is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the ground state of an atom so that it is completely detached from the atom (n = ); for hydrogen it is 13.6 eV.
Spectral series of hydrogen: Lyman (transitions to n = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (to n = 2, visible), Paschen (to n = 3, infrared).
Laser action: stimulated emission produces photons identical in phase, frequency and direction to the stimulating photon; population inversion is needed for light amplification.
Hydrogen energy levels: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV; a photon is emitted when the electron drops to a lower level.
Hydrogen energy levels · Eₙ = −(13.6)/(n²) eV · n = 1, 2, 3, … (n = 1 is the ground state); Eₙ = energy of level n (eV); 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Photon emitted or absorbed in a transition · hf = hc/λ = E_i − E_f · E_i = energy of the initial (higher) level (J); E_f = energy of the final level (J); f = photon frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m)
Rydberg formula · 1/λ = R((1)/(n_f²) − (1)/(n_i²)) · R = 1.10 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ (Rydberg constant); λ = wavelength (m); n_i = initial level; n_f = final level
Bohr radius of orbit · rₙ = n² a₀ · rₙ = radius of the nth orbit (m); a₀ = 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m (Bohr radius); n = 1, 2, 3, …
Write the energies of both levels using −(13.6)/(n²) (or the value calculated from the data given), subtract (higher − lower) to obtain a positive photon energy, convert eV to J, then λ = hc/E.
Explain line spectra in 2 points: electrons have only discrete energy levels; photons emitted in transitions have energy equal to the difference of two levels, so only specific wavelengths appear.
Name the series (Lyman/Balmer/Paschen) and the region of the spectrum when asked.
Give the wavelength in nm to 3 s.f. and the energy in eV.
For ionisation energy, start from E = E − E₁ = 0 − E₁, then substitute. Writing only "−E₁" can lose the mark.
Calculator: (me⁴)/(8ε₀²h²n²) gives 0 if keyed in one go, because intermediate powers go beyond 10⁻⁹⁹. Evaluate in steps (m ÷ 8 ÷ ε₀², then × e⁴, then ÷ h², then ÷ n²).
Do not assume Eₙ = −(13.6)/(n²) eV is exact for every question. When asked to calculate, use the constants given; the result may be, for example, −13.58 eV.
X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁹ m), produced when fast electrons are suddenly stopped by a metal target.

Continuous spectrum arises from the deceleration of electrons in the target (bremsstrahlung); it has a sharp cut-off at the minimum wavelength λ_min, corresponding to the whole kinetic energy of an electron being converted to a single photon.

Characteristic spectrum consists of sharp lines produced when an incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron of the target atom and an outer electron falls to fill the vacancy; the lines are characteristic of the target material.
Bragg's law: constructive interference occurs for X-rays reflected from successive crystal planes when the path difference 2d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths.
Glancing angle θ is the angle between the incident X-ray beam and the atomic (crystal) plane.
Intensity of the X-ray beam depends on the tube current; the penetrating power (hardness) depends on the accelerating voltage.
X-ray spectrum: a continuous spectrum starting at λmin = hc/eV, plus sharp characteristic lines of the target.

Kinetic energy of electron at target · eV = ½mv² · electron reaching the target from rest; V = accelerating potential difference (V); e = electron charge (C); m = electron mass (kg); v = speed at the target (m s⁻¹)
Minimum wavelength · eV = (hc)/(λ_min); λ_min = hc/eV · λ_min = minimum wavelength (m); h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; V = accelerating potential difference (V)
Bragg's law · 2d sin θ = nλ · d = spacing of the crystal planes (m); θ = glancing angle (measured from the planes, not the normal); n = 1, 2, 3, … (order); λ = wavelength (m)
Attenuation of X-rays · I = I₀ e^−μx · I₀ = incident intensity (W m⁻²); I = transmitted intensity (W m⁻²); μ = linear attenuation coefficient (m⁻¹); x = thickness of the absorber (m)
For λ_min write λ_min = hc/eV, substitute with units; state that λ_min depends only on V and not on the target material.
For Bragg's law, state that θ is the glancing angle between the beam and the crystal planes; write 2d sin θ = nλ and solve.
For the characteristic lines, state 'transition of an outer electron to a vacancy in an inner shell'.
When asked for the electron speed, equate eV to ½mv² and convert kV to V.

Continuous spectrum: high-speed electrons decelerate in the target; an electron that loses all its kinetic energy in one (head-on) collision emits the photon of minimum wavelength; electrons that lose their energy in several collisions emit photons of lower frequencies, giving a continuous range.

Characteristic spectrum: state energetic (high-speed) electrons accelerated by a high p.d.; they penetrate the target atoms and knock out inner orbital electrons, creating vacancies; electrons from higher energy levels fall to fill the vacancies and release X-ray photons of definite energies. Without "energetic" the first mark is lost.

X-ray production is the inverse of the photoelectric effect: in X-ray production the kinetic energy of electrons is converted to photons; in the photoelectric effect a photon’s energy is converted to the kinetic energy of an electron.
Glancing angle θ (Bragg, 2d sin θ = mλ) is half of the angle between the incident and diffracted beams (2θ); do not confuse it with the diffraction angle in d sin θ = mλ for a grating.
Nanoscience is the study of materials and structures with at least one dimension of the order of 1 nm to 100 nm.
The surface-area-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles is very large, so a large proportion of atoms lie at the surface, which gives a high chemical reactivity and catalytic activity.

Scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) uses the quantum-mechanical tunnelling current between a sharp conducting tip and the surface; the current depends very sensitively (exponentially) on the tip–surface separation, so atoms can be imaged.
Examples: carbon nanotubes (high strength, electrical conduction), graphene, nanoparticles in sunscreens and catalysts.
Nanoscience works at 1–100 nm, where the large surface-area-to-volume ratio changes a material's properties.
Surface area to volume ratio of a sphere · 3/r · r = radius of the sphere (m); ratio in m⁻¹; the ratio increases as the size decreases
Surface area to volume ratio of a cube · 6/L · L = side of the cube (m); ratio in m⁻¹; the ratio increases as the size decreases
1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m; the nanoscale is about 1–100 nm.
For reactivity state: smaller particles have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio, so more atoms are exposed at the surface.
For STM state: tunnelling current → very sensitive to the separation → used to map the surface atom by atom.
Give the nanoscale range as 1 nm to 100 nm.

Know everyday applications (miniaturisation of devices, memory storage, OLED displays in phones and TVs). The main aims of nanotechnology: make devices faster and lighter and save energy; use this to pick the correct option.
The nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m across) contains protons and neutrons, together called nucleons.

Proton: Rutherford (1919) bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles and found that hydrogen nuclei were knocked out. He identified this positively charged particle, present in every nucleus, as the proton.
Neutron: Chadwick (1932) showed that the radiation produced when beryllium is bombarded with alpha particles consists of uncharged particles with a mass close to that of the proton: neutrons.
Proton number (atomic number) Z: the number of protons in the nucleus.
Nucleon number (mass number) A: the total number of protons and neutrons. Number of neutrons N = A − Z.
A nuclide is written ^A_ZX, e.g. ⁵⁶₂₆Fe has 26 protons and 30 neutrons.
Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, e.g. hydrogen ¹₁H, deuterium ²₁H and tritium ³₁H.
Positive ions pass through a velocity selector with perpendicular fields E and B₁. Only ions with qE = qvB₁, i.e. v = E/B₁, go straight through.
In the uniform field B₂ the ions move in semicircles: qvB₂ = mv²/r, so r = (mE)/(qB₁B₂) ∝ m.
Isotopes of different mass land at different places on the plate: m₁/m₂ = r₁/r₂. It is used to measure atomic masses and the abundance of isotopes.
Mass defect, Δmthe difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
Binding energy, E_Bthe energy needed to separate a nucleus completely into its individual protons and neutrons. It is also the energy released when the nucleus is formed from its nucleons.
Unified atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
Its energy equivalent: E = (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 1.49 × 10⁻¹⁰ J = 931.5 MeV.
Figure 26.2: binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number.
Binding energy per nucleon = E_B/A. It measures the stability of a nucleus: the larger it is, the more tightly bound and stable the nucleus.
For light nuclei it rises rapidly with A (helium-4 is unusually stable, a peak at 7.1 MeV).
It is largest, about 8.8 MeV, for A ≈ 56–62 (iron and nickel): the most stable nuclei.
For heavier nuclei it decreases slowly, to about 7.6 MeV for uranium.
Energy is released when nuclei move towards the peak: light nuclei fuse, heavy nuclei split (fission).
Move along the curve to see how tightly bound each nucleus is. Then try a fission of uranium and a fusion of hydrogen: both move the nucleons up the curve and release energy.
Radioactivityis the spontaneous and random emission of radiation (α, β or γ) from unstable nuclei, forming a new nucleus.
Spontaneous: the decay happens on its own and is not affected by physical conditions (temperature, pressure) or chemical changes.

Random: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay; every nucleus has the same probability of decaying per unit time. Only the behaviour of a large number of nuclei can be predicted.

Each square is a nucleus. Every tick each one has the same small chance of decaying, so you cannot tell which will go next, yet the total follows N = N₀e^(−λt). Change the half-life and the number of nuclei, and compare the count with the curve.
A radioisotope behaves chemically like the stable isotope, so it can be followed by detecting its radiation. Short half-lives are chosen so that the activity soon dies away.
Medical: blood volume · a small known activity is injected; after it mixes, the activity per unit volume of a blood sample gives the total volume
Medical: imaging · technetium-99m (γ emitter, half-life 6 h) collects in tumours, which then show up on a gamma camera; iodine-131 is used for the thyroid
Agriculture · phosphorus-32 in fertiliser shows how fast and where the plant takes it up; tracers also study pesticides and are used in the sterile insect technique
Industry · a short-lived tracer in an underground pipe: a Geiger counter above the ground detects higher activity where the pipe leaks; also thickness gauges and flow measurement
A nuclear reaction changes the nucleus: radioactive decay, bombardment by a particle, fission or fusion. For example, Rutherford’s first artificial reaction: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H.
Conservation of nucleon number: the total nucleon number A before the reaction equals the total after.
Conservation of charge: the total proton number (charge) Z before equals the total after.
Conservation of mass–energy: the total mass-energy (rest mass energy + kinetic energy) before equals the total after. Any loss of mass appears as energy.
Nuclear fissionis the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei of roughly equal mass, with the release of neutrons and energy.
Fission of uranium-235 is usually induced by a slow (thermal) neutron. The excited U-236 nucleus splits within about 10⁻¹² s.
The fragments vary, mostly with A about 90–100 and 135–145.

Why energy is released: the binding energy per nucleon of uranium is about 7.6 MeV, but that of the fragments is about 8.5 MeV. The products are more tightly bound, so they have less mass. Energy released ≈ (8.5 − 7.6) × 236 ≈ 200 MeV per fission, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons.
Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons. If at least one of them causes another fission, the reaction continues by itself: a chain reaction.

If the piece of uranium is too small, too many neutrons escape through the surface and the chain dies out. The critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material needed to sustain a chain reaction.
Above the critical mass, if every neutron is allowed to cause fission, the number of fissions grows very rapidly (an uncontrolled chain reaction, as in a bomb).

Controlled fission in a nuclear reactor

Fire one neutron into the uranium. Each fission (yellow nucleus) releases 2–3 new neutrons. Push the control rods in to absorb more neutrons: find the setting where the reaction keeps going at a steady rate.
The fission energy heats the water in the reactor core. In a pressurised water reactor the water is kept at high pressure so it does not boil, and the same water acts as moderator and coolant.
The hot coolant is pumped through a heat exchanger (steam generator), where it boils water in a separate loop. The steam turns a turbine connected to a generator.
The steam is cooled back to water in a condenser and returned. Only about one third of the heat becomes electrical energy; the rest is given out to the cooling water.
If the power rises too fast, the control rods drop fully into the core (an emergency shutdown) and the chain reaction stops.

Move the control rods. Pulled out, more neutrons survive and the power rises; pushed in, the power falls. Find the position where each fission causes, on average, exactly one more (k = 1) and the power stays steady. If the power goes above 120%, the reactor shuts itself down.
Nuclear fusionis the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, with the release of energy.

Light nuclei have a low binding energy per nucleon. The product (e.g. helium-4) is much more tightly bound, so mass is lost and energy is released. Per nucleon, fusion releases more energy than fission.

The nuclei are both positive and repel each other. To come within the range of the strong nuclear force (about 10⁻¹⁵ m) they need very high kinetic energies, i.e. temperatures of about 10⁷–10⁸ K. Fusion is therefore called a thermonuclear reaction.
The Sun’s core has a temperature of about 1.5 × 10⁷ K and a very high density, so hydrogen nuclei collide fast and often enough to fuse.
The main process is the proton–proton chain:
a heavy nucleus splits into lighter ones · light nuclei join into a heavier one
started by neutron bombardment · needs a very high temperature
produces radioactive waste · products mostly not radioactive
controlled in reactors today · very difficult to contain and control
Both release energy, both produce new nuclei, and in both the total mass decreases.
Low-level (gloves, clothing, tools) · sealed in drums and buried in shallow engineered landfill sites
Intermediate-level · mixed with concrete or bitumen in steel containers, stored in deep vaults

High-level (used fuel) · cooled for years under water, then sealed in thick steel and concrete casks for deep geological burial, away from groundwater and earthquake zones; some is reprocessed to recover uranium and plutonium

The four marking points for the definition
An unstable nucleus emits α, β or γ radiation.
It becomes a different, more stable daughter nuclide.
The decay is spontaneous: it is not affected by physical conditions such as temperature and pressure.
The rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei.
The decay is random: we cannot predict which nucleus decays next, only the fraction that decays.
The proton (atomic) number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus; the nucleon (mass) number A is the total number of protons and neutrons; the number of neutrons N = A − Z.
Isotopes are nuclides of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A).
A nuclide is a particular species of nucleus with a specified proton number Z and nucleon number A.
The unified atomic mass unit (u) is one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg ≡ 931.5 MeV.
The mass defect is the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.
The binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons; B = Δmc².

The binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons. It is a measure of nuclear stability: a nucleus with a greater binding energy per nucleon is more stable; the curve rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks at about 8.8 MeV near ⁵⁶Fe (A ≈ 56) and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.
The nuclear radius R = R₀A^1/3, so the nuclear density is the same for all nuclei (about 2×10¹⁷ kg m⁻³).
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56: light nuclei release energy by fusion, heavy nuclei by fission.

Radioactive decay is the spontaneous and random disintegration of an unstable nucleus with the emission of α, β or γ radiation.

Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous. Random: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, and every nucleus has the same probability of decay per unit time. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external physical conditions such as temperature and pressure.
The activity A is the rate of decay of the nuclei, A = −dN/dt = λN, measured in becquerel (Bq; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second).
The decay constant λ is the probability of decay per unit time of a nucleus.
The half-life t½ is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to fall to half of its initial value.
α emission reduces A by 4 and Z by 2; β⁻ emission raises Z by 1 with A unchanged; γ emission changes neither A nor Z.
Radioactive decay: N = N₀e^(−λt); the number halves every half-life.
Decay law · N = N₀e^−λt; A = A₀e^−λt · N = number of undecayed nuclei; A = activity (Bq); N₀, A₀ = values at t = 0; λ = decay constant (s⁻¹); t = time (s)
Half-life · t½ = (ln 2)/(λ) = (0.693)/(λ) · t½ = half-life (s); λ = decay constant (s⁻¹)

Activity · A = λN; A ∝ N · A = activity (Bq); λ = decay constant (s⁻¹); N = number of undecayed nuclei
Linearised decay law · ln A = ln A₀ − λt · A = activity (Bq); A₀ = initial activity (Bq); λ = decay constant (s⁻¹); t = time (s); graph of ln A against t is a straight line with gradient −λ
Convert the half-life to seconds when the activity is required in Bq: t½ in s → λ = (ln 2)/(t½) → A = λN.
State the number of half-lives n = t/t½ first, then fraction = (½)ⁿ; non-integer n is allowed with the exponential form.
Show the substitution, the evaluated result to 3 s.f., and the unit (Bq, s⁻¹ or mass in the unit asked).
For explanation questions, state 'random and spontaneous' and refer to constant probability of decay per unit time.
In a nuclear reaction, mass number, charge (atomic number), energy and momentum are conserved; rest mass is not conserved.
The Q-value of a reaction is the energy released (Q > 0) or absorbed (Q < 0), Q = (total mass of reactants − total mass of products)c².

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (e.g. ²³⁵U, after absorbing a neutron) into two lighter nuclei with the release of energy and neutrons; each fission of ²³⁵U releases about 200 MeV.
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus with the release of energy; it requires a very high temperature to overcome electrostatic repulsion.
Energy is released in fission and fusion because the products have a greater binding energy per nucleon, so their total mass is less than that of the reactants.
A chain reaction is sustained when, on average, at least one of the secondary neutrons from each fission causes another fission.

A thermal neutron is a slow neutron whose kinetic energy is about the same as the thermal energy of particles at room temperature (about 0.025 eV); thermal neutrons are the most likely to cause fission of ²³⁵U.

A thermonuclear reaction is a fusion reaction that occurs when the temperature of the light nuclei is raised to about 10⁸ K, so that they collide with enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion and fuse.
Nuclear reactions conserve nucleon number and charge; the mass defect is released as energy Q = Δmc².
Q-value of a reaction · Q = Δmc² = (Σm_reactants − Σm_products) × 931.5 MeV · Q = energy released (MeV); Δm = mass difference (u); masses in u; c = speed of light
Mass-energy equivalence · E = Δmc² · E = energy (J); Δm = mass difference (kg); c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹; 1 u = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg
Nuclear equation · ΣA and ΣZ equal on both sides; e.g. ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n · A = nucleon number; Z = proton number; both conserved in a nuclear reaction
Power from fission · P = (fission rate) × (energy per fission) · P = power (W); fission rate in s⁻¹; energy per fission in J
Mass of ²³⁵U used · Mass = (number of fissions × 235 g)/(N_A) · Mass in g; N_A = Avogadro constant (mol⁻¹)
